The air was full of the rich, mellow fragrance of wine. The fire in the little red-clay stove was small, yet just enough to turn that grim, cold hollow in the mountain warm and snug.
Lu Xiaofeng sighed softly. "I've come to the right place after all, and just at the right time."
Huo Xiu sighed too. "What I can't fathom," he said, "is how a man like you always contrives to find me the very moment I've good wine to drink."
He turned his head, smiling; and the pair of bright eyes in that failing old face made him seem full of life yet. "If you don't mind dirtying your clothes," he said, "sit down and have a cup."

Lu Xiaofeng looked down at his own bright-red cloak, then at the old clothes on the other man, washed white with age, and could not help laughing. "When I've as much put by as you, I'll dress like that too."
"Oh?" said Huo Xiu.
"Only a great rich man like you is fit to wear such clothes," said Lu Xiaofeng. "I'm not fit for them yet."
"Why?" said Huo Xiu.
"Because once a man is truly rich," said Lu Xiaofeng, "it makes no difference at all what he wears."
Huo Xiu smiled. "The pity is, you'll never be rich."
"Why?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Because you're too clever," said Huo Xiu. "Men who are too clever never grow rich."
"But the last time we met," said Lu Xiaofeng, "you said I'd make my fortune sooner or later."
"That was only because I hadn't yet found out how clever you were," said Huo Xiu.
"And when did you find that out?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Just now," said Huo Xiu.
Lu Xiaofeng laughed again.
"Save you," said Huo Xiu, "I doubt there's a second man alive who could have found his way in here so smoothly."
Lu Xiaofeng laughed. "Is that because no one else is as biddable as I'm?"

Huo Xiu nodded. "Of ten men who saw the word Push on that door, nine at least wouldn't push it, and a man who won't push it never gets in at all. See the word Turn and fail to turn, and no one alive gets out again from my nine-fold maze. See the word Stop and fail to stop, and even if the arrows don't leave you a hedgehog, you'll lose a layer of skin in the oil-cauldron."

"But the deadliest of all," said Lu Xiaofeng, "was surely the soul-stealing incense in that room above. It all but overcame even Hua Manlou. Few men, I think, could have guessed that those two bowls of wine held not poison but its cure."
"Yet you guessed it," said Huo Xiu.
Lu Xiaofeng smiled. "I only knew that, good or bad, you're not a man to let a friend walk into a trap; for you've precious few friends, and every one that dies is one the fewer."
Huo Xiu fixed his bright eyes on him, and after a long while asked of a sudden, "What else do you know?"
Lu Xiaofeng gazed back at him, and after a long while said slowly, "I know, too, that your surname was never Huo. Your name at the first was Shangguan Mu."
Huo Xiu's face did not change in the least. "Just so," he said lightly.
"You and Yan Tieshan and Dugu Yihe," said Lu Xiaofeng, "were once great ministers of the kingdom of the Golden Roc, all three."
"Just so," said Huo Xiu.
His face was calm still, without the least trace of guilt or remorse.

Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "But then greed got the better of good faith, and you swallowed the fortune whole. The moment you reached the Central Lands you went to ground, and never kept the tryst to seek out that thirteenth-generation King of the Golden Roc—"
Huo Xiu cut him short. "You're wrong."
Lu Xiaofeng frowned. "Wrong?"
"Wrong in this one thing," said Huo Xiu.
"Which thing?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"It wasn't we who broke the tryst," said Huo Xiu, "but the young prince, who fled into exile at Shangguan Jin's side."
Lu Xiaofeng was struck dumb. This, truly, was a thing he had never thought of; he did not believe it at all.
"Not only did he fail to wait for us at the place appointed," said Huo Xiu, "he hid himself from us the whole while. We searched tens of years, and never found him."
"So by your account," said Lu Xiaofeng, "it wasn't you hiding from him, but he from you?"
"Just so," said Huo Xiu.

"You were the ministers his royal father charged with his keeping," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and you carried a great fortune that was his by right. Why should he hide from you? Was there something amiss with the man?"
Huo Xiu said coldly, "Because the fortune wasn't his. It belonged to the kingdom of the Golden Roc."
"And what difference does that make?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"A difference, and a great one," said Huo Xiu.
"Oh?" said Lu Xiaofeng.

"Had he taken the fortune to himself," said Huo Xiu, "he must then have used it to win back the throne the Golden Roc had lost; and that is no easy thing. It means bitter hardship, and a man's life in danger at every turn."

Lu Xiaofeng granted it: to be born into a royal house is not always good fortune. "Would that, life upon life, I were never again born into a king's house," runs the old cry, and its bitterness is not a thing common men can feel.
A helpless sorrow came of a sudden into Huo Xiu's eyes, and he said slowly, "The pity is that our young prince was no Tian Dan, no Emperor Guangwu."
Lu Xiaofeng could not help asking, "What manner of man was he?"
"He was a poet, like Li Houzhu," said Huo Xiu, "and a painter, like the Emperor Huizong of Song; from boyhood men called him a master of the three perfections, poetry and calligraphy and painting."

He sighed, and went on: "A man like that is a quiet soul by nature. Win the throne or lose it, he cared nothing either way, likely; he wished only to wander free with his verses and his wine, and live out his days in peace. And besides—"
"Besides what?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Shangguan Jin's own wealth," said Huo Xiu, "was enough to keep them in ease a lifetime already."
Lu Xiaofeng said no more; but to say no more did not mean that he believed it.
"You don't believe me?" said Huo Xiu.
Lu Xiaofeng still said nothing.
"The war-chest and the arms we laid by to raise the Golden Roc again," said Huo Xiu, "you'll have seen them just now."
Lu Xiaofeng nodded.

"With the Golden Roc's fortune we did indeed make a great deal more," said Huo Xiu; "but that was only so we might use it to win over the great ministers of your own court, and borrow soldiers to march. Yet without the young prince, what cause had we to march at all?"
His words had plainly left Lu Xiaofeng no room for doubt; yet Lu Xiaofeng could not help asking, "If he truly hid from you all this while, why should he seek you out now, all at once?"
Huo Xiu said coldly, "It isn't as though no one had ever come seeking us before."
"Oh?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Those four old men outside," said Huo Xiu, "you'll have seen them just now."
Understanding broke over Lu Xiaofeng. "You mean they're all impostors, each passing himself off as the Great King of the Golden Roc, to seize the fortune?"

Huo Xiu nodded. "They wanted riches, so I set them before gold and jewels from dawn to dark. They wanted to play at kingship, so I let them sit a throne in dragon-robes the day long. They came to cheat me of my wealth; yet I haven't used them ill."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed, and smiled wryly. "It seems you're no gentleman either. No gentleman would ever deal with men so."
Though in truth he could not but own that, for men of that stamp, no fitter way could be found.
"This was a great secret," said Huo Xiu. "Save the four of us and the young prince, no one should have known it at all."
"Then how came they to know it?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"They didn't," said Huo Xiu.
Lu Xiaofeng was struck dumb; he could make no sense of the words.
"The one who knew the secret," said Huo Xiu, "was another man altogether; they were no more than the puppets he worked."
"And who is this man?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I don't know," said Huo Xiu.
"They don't know either?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu smiled coldly. "Were you this man, would you show your true face to anyone?"
Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly. "I wouldn't."
"They saw the man but three times in all," said Huo Xiu, "and his face was different at every meeting. Had his voice not stayed the same, they would never have believed it was the one man."
"So the man not only lays his plans with care," said Lu Xiaofeng, "but is a past master of the art of disguise."
Hua Manlou, who had listened in silence all the while, said of a sudden, "A true master of disguise can change even his voice."
"Oh?" said Lu Xiaofeng.

"The art of disguise is what they call ninjutsu, on the three isles of Fusang in the Eastern Sea," said Hua Manlou. "There is a discipline within it that, once mastered, lets a man govern the very muscles of his throat and change the sound of his speech utterly."
"So that not even you could tell?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"If the discipline is brought to its perfection," said Hua Manlou, "not even I could tell."
Lu Xiaofeng pondered. "You mean the Great King of the Golden Roc who summoned us this time may be a counterfeit too!"
"I sent Sikong Zhaixing to steal the Princess Danfeng away," said Huo Xiu, "for no reason but to learn whether the man was true or false; and the pity is that he happens to be a friend of yours."
"As well, then, that you brought it off in the end," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and that Shangguan Danfeng fell into your hands after all."
"Who says she fell into my hands?" said Huo Xiu.
Lu Xiaofeng frowned. "She didn't?"
"She didn't," said Huo Xiu.
Lu Xiaofeng was struck dumb again. He knew Huo Xiu for no liar.
And if what Huo Xiu said was no lie, how had Shangguan Danfeng come to vanish so suddenly? He could not fathom it. No one could.
"To this very hour," said Huo Xiu, "I've never once set eyes on the woman."
"And Shangguan Feiyan, her you've never seen either?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"That name I haven't so much as heard," said Huo Xiu.

Lu Xiaofeng was more at a loss than ever; the tangled, treacherous turns of the affair had gone clean past anything he had looked for. He smiled wryly. "Small wonder Yan Tieshan was so quick to drive me off, the moment he heard I knew the secret. He must have taken me for one of the plot, come to seize the fortune with the rest."
"Whereas you took it," said Huo Xiu, "for the fury of a man whose secret has been laid bare."

Lu Xiaofeng could only own it. And now, at last, he understood the strange look on Yan Tieshan's face as he lay dying, gazing at Shangguan Danfeng. But could Shangguan Danfeng truly be a murderess, killing for gain?

Still he could not believe it. If the whole thing were a fraud, why had so many sought to keep him from meddling in it? Why had the Blue-Robe Tower sent men to stop him ever meeting the Great King of the Golden Roc?
Hua Manlou said of a sudden, "When did you last see this young prince?"
"More than forty years ago," said Huo Xiu.
"And how old was he then?" said Hua Manlou.
"Thirteen," said Huo Xiu.
"Forty years and more have passed," said Hua Manlou; "the prince who was thirteen then is a man in his dotage now."
Huo Xiu heaved a long sigh. "The years are pitiless. Every man must grow old."
"Then how can you tell," said Hua Manlou, "whether an old man of sixty now is the very prince who was thirteen then?"
Huo Xiu pondered. "There is a secret in that too, a secret no other soul has ever known."
Hua Manlou asked no more; he held that every man has a right to keep his own secrets.
But Huo Xiu went on regardless: "Yet I trust the two of you, and so I'm willing to tell it you."
Hua Manlou answered with a silence that was gratitude; the trust of a man like Huo Xiu was no easy thing to win.
"Every king of the Golden Roc, generation upon generation," said Huo Xiu, "is born with a mark past nature: upon each foot he bears six toes."
Understanding broke over Lu Xiaofeng. "So it was by this that you knew the four old men outside for counterfeits."
Huo Xiu nodded. "Even a man who knew the secret would be hard put to counterfeit it. A man with six toes on both feet, I've never seen a second one to this day."
Lu Xiaofeng laughed. "I've never seen even the one."
Huo Xiu smiled. "Men with four eyebrows are none so common either."
Lu Xiaofeng laughed too.
"So now," said Huo Xiu, "you've only to find some way to draw off the Great King's boots and count the toes on his feet, and you'll know the true from the false."
"That's easily done," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu smiled. "Drawing off a man's boots is at least easier than drawing off a woman's breeches."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "It seems you're truly no gentleman. Not in the least."
Huo Xiu sighed in his turn. "It is no hard thing to be a gentleman. To be a scoundrel such as I'm, there is the hard thing."
Lu Xiaofeng took his meaning. Whoever had so vast a fortune to guard could not but meet the world, first of all, with a scoundrel's wariness.
Huo Xiu said again, "If this Great King of the Golden Roc should truly be the prince of those years, I may at last set down the burden off my shoulders. If not—"
"If not," said Lu Xiaofeng, "I'll bring him here as well, to keep the four old men company."

When they walked out of that secret hollow in the mountain it was near dawn. The spring wind was cold and clean, the green hills deep with green, and the dew on the grass, in the first light, shone clearer and brighter far than any pearl. The world was a lovely thing yet.
Lu Xiaofeng drew a deep breath, and smiled wryly. "My foreboding was right after all. Today I've met with another strange thing indeed."
The way the affair had unfolded and turned was truly past any man's imagining.
Hua Manlou said of a sudden, "Do you think there could truly be a man in this world with six toes on both his feet?"
"I don't know," said Lu Xiaofeng. "I've never seen one."

"If there is no such man in the world at all," said Hua Manlou, "then we'll never find the true Great King of the Golden Roc; and even were what Huo Xiu says a lie, would it not thereby become the truth?"
Lu Xiaofeng pondered, then smiled of a sudden. "I know only that this is a world where nothing is too strange to be, with every manner of queer and marvellous man already in it."
Hua Manlou laughed too. "Just so. If a man may have four eyebrows, why not six toes? The pity is that of your own four eyebrows, only two are left."
Lu Xiaofeng ran a finger over his upper lip, and smiled. "This time, again, you're wrong."
"How so?" said Hua Manlou.
"A moustache, howsoever close it's shaved," said Lu Xiaofeng, "will grow back all the same."
No sooner had he said it than he saw a figure come drifting like a ghost out of the mist-hung wood.
Her face was pale, worn and wan; yet she was beautiful still.
Lu Xiaofeng knew her. "Miss Ye, Ye Xiuzhu?"
Ye Xiuzhu nodded.
"Are you waiting here for someone, Miss Ye?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Ye Xiuzhu shook her head. "I've been here all last night."
"Why?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Ye Xiuzhu said, low and sorrowful, "We buried our master here, and our youngest sister; our eldest sister was worn out, and I, I couldn't sleep."
She was indeed the most guileless of the Four Beauties of Emei; set her before a man, and she could scarce get a word out.
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. For this girl he felt, in truth, a real sorrow; and he did not know what to say.
But Ye Xiuzhu spoke again, of a sudden: "We never caught up with Ximen Chuixue; and so, so now we don't even know whether our Third Sister is alive or dead."
"I'll go and bring her back to you," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Ye Xiuzhu bowed her head lower still, and after a long while said softly, "There is one thing more I must tell you."
Lu Xiaofeng waited for her to go on.

Ye Xiuzhu said, "This was a thing our Third Sister meant to tell you; but before she could speak it out, she was already, she was already—" Her voice broke of a sudden; quietly she wiped the tear-tracks with her sleeve before she went on: "Our master came to Guanzhong this time for one reason only, that word had reached him the First Blue-Robe Tower stands on the mountain behind the Pavilion of Pearls and Splendour."
Lu Xiaofeng could not help saying, "No man's news is ever bound to be right in every part."

Ye Xiuzhu lifted her head sharply. "But it was for these very words that our Third Sister was struck down. Plainly someone didn't want them spoken; and so I hold they must be of great weight, and I've come to tell you." Grief and anger showed in her face, and her voice had risen.
Again Lu Xiaofeng felt the pang of sorrow, and smiled wryly. "I know you mean it kindly. Whatever comes, if I get to the bottom of this, I'll come and tell you first."
Ye Xiuzhu bowed her head once more, and after a long silence asked softly, "Where will you go now?"
"We're going to look on a man with six toes upon his foot," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Ye Xiuzhu raised her head again, staring at him in astonishment, then turned of a sudden and walked quickly away.
Hua Manlou sighed. "I think she must take you for a madman now."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed too, and smiled wryly. "Even I'm beginning to think myself a little mad."
The long corridor was dark and still. They waited at the end of it, while someone went in ahead to announce them to the Great King of the Golden Roc.
Hua Manlou could not help murmuring, "Do you think you can be sure of getting his boots off?"
"No," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Have you hit on any way to do it?" said Hua Manlou.
"I've hit on plenty," said Lu Xiaofeng, "only I can't tell which to use."
"Name me two of them," said Hua Manlou.
"I could knock over a pot of water on purpose and spill it on his feet," said Lu Xiaofeng; "or I could praise his boots for handsome ones and ask him to draw them off so I might look."
Hua Manlou frowned. "Don't you know how foolish such tricks are?"
Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly. "Of course I know it. But the whole business is a foolish one; how should I hit on a clever way to do a foolish thing?"
He said no more, for at that the door had opened.

The Great King of the Golden Roc sat still in that broad, comfortable chair; his face was eager, and impatient, and before they had so much as come in he demanded, "You've found the three traitor-ministers?"
"Only two of them," said Lu Xiaofeng.
The Great King's eyes lit up. "And where are they?"
"Dead already," said Lu Xiaofeng.
The Great King's face changed. "How came they to die?"

Lu Xiaofeng answered somewhat absently, for he had not yet caught sight of the Great King's feet. Over the Great King's knees lay a thin coverlet worked with golden dragons, as though he felt the cold keenly.

But Hua Manlou had already set out the plain course of it, and added, "We never found Huo Xiu; he is a hard man to find at the best of times." It was the first lie of his life, and he found of a sudden that lying was no very difficult thing.
For as he told the lie, he felt in his heart that he had wronged no one by it.
The Great King heaved a long sigh, and said with hatred, "I had meant to see them once, to see whether they still had the face to meet my eyes."
Hua Manlou said of a sudden, "There is one I should like to see now, myself."
"Who?" said the Great King.
"Zhu Ting," said Hua Manlou.
The Great King frowned. "I was about to ask you of him. Twice I've sent to fetch him, and twice he hasn't come."
Hua Manlou mused, and smiled at last. "That may be only because he is a lazy man by nature."
Lu Xiaofeng said of a sudden, "The dragon worked on this coverlet is a fine one, near enough to the life."

It was a foolish thing to say, and he followed it with a foolish thing to do: he lifted the coverlet clean away, and then, like a very fool, he stood there dumbstruck. Below the Great King's trouser-hems was nothing at all; both his legs had been cut away above the knee.
"You wonder, do you," said the Great King, "how my legs come to be gone all of a sudden?"
Lu Xiaofeng could only nod, and smile wryly.

The Great King sighed. "There was always something amiss with my legs; a cup of wine, and they pained me past bearing. An old man has ailments enough." That much was true; Lu Xiaofeng had known it on his last visit.
The Great King smiled wryly. "But what pleasure has an old man like me, beyond his wine?"
Lu Xiaofeng forced a smile. "So, so you drank again, in secret?"

"I thought a little would do no harm," said the Great King; "but who could have known that, three cups down, both my legs swelled up and festered to the bone. So, so I had Liu Yuhen cut the two of them off and be done."

He burst of a sudden into laughter. "Legless as I'm now, I can drink in peace at last. This very night I'll take the two of you on, and see whether an old man's head for wine can still match you young fellows."
Lu Xiaofeng could only look at him and smile wryly.

"Had you come a few days sooner," said the Great King, "I'd have shown you the two legs I had off, so you might see that, old as I'm, I've the mettle yet of the brave man who, snake-bitten on the hand, strikes off his own wrist."
Lu Xiaofeng could not help asking, "And where are the two legs now?"
"I've burned them," said the Great King.
Lu Xiaofeng started. "Burned them? Why burn them?"
"These two legs kept me ten years from my wine," said the Great King. "Was I to burn them, or set them up on an altar with flowers and fine wine to worship?"
Lu Xiaofeng had no words. Looking on the proud, self-satisfied look on the old man's face, he felt of a sudden that he grew more and more the simpleton.
A simpleton, and a fool.
The long corridor was dark and grim as before; slowly they walked out of it.
Hua Manlou smiled of a sudden. "Well, you've solved one hard problem at least."
"Oh?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"You needn't rack your brains to get his boots off now," said Hua Manlou, "for he has no boots at all."
Lu Xiaofeng said coldly, "When did you turn so droll?"
But there was nothing droll in it at all. Now not even Huo Xiu could tell whether this Great King of the Golden Roc were true or false.
To call it mere chance, he could hardly believe the world held a chance so neat.

And to call it no chance, then how had the Great King known the secret? They had come straight here from Huo Xiu's little tower; unless the Great King had eyes that saw a thousand li and ears that caught the wind, how could he have known they were coming to look at his feet?
Lu Xiaofeng sighed again. "If a cup of wine made my legs swell, I might have the two of them off as well."
Hua Manlou sighed. "There seem to be no few men in this world who'd risk their lives for the drink."
Lu Xiaofeng said of a sudden, "That room will still be kept for you; why not go in and sleep a while? Don't forget they mean to drink you under the table tonight."
"And you?" said Hua Manlou.
"I'm off to find someone," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Find who?" said Hua Manlou.
"A woman, of course," said Lu Xiaofeng. "A woman with feet."
Hua Manlou's face lit of a sudden. "Just so. You should go quickly and find a woman with six toes upon her foot."
"Oh?" said Lu Xiaofeng.

"Don't forget that every trueborn child of the Golden Roc line, generation on generation, has six toes upon the foot," said Hua Manlou; "it runs in their blood. And since Shangguan Danfeng is the Great King's own daughter, she too should have six toes; so you—"
He said no more, for he found of a sudden that Lu Xiaofeng was already gone.
Near dusk, but not yet dusk. The flowers in the garden bloomed bright as ever, and the wind was full of their scent; but not a soul was to be seen.
Shangguan Xue'er was not in the garden. It was not Shangguan Danfeng that Lu Xiaofeng sought, for he knew Shangguan Danfeng would never be here.
That the Great King had not once asked after his daughter's whereabouts, that too was a very strange thing.
But Lu Xiaofeng had no leisure to think on it now; he wanted only to find Shangguan Xue'er quickly, for he had a thing to ask Shangguan Xue'er, a thing of great weight.

When he had no wish to find her, she was forever flitting about before his eyes; now that he wanted her in haste, the little sprite was nowhere to be seen. Lu Xiaofeng sighed, and passing along the little path among the flowers came all at once upon a side gate.
The gate stood ajar; behind it was a small courtyard, and in the courtyard a well.
He pushed it open and went in, and there at last he found Shangguan Xue'er; the little sprite seemed always to delight in queer and out-of-the-way doings.
Now here she was, crouched alone in the courtyard, her two great eyes fixed unblinking on a patch of bare ground before her, as though lost in it.
Yet on the ground there was nothing at all, not so much as a blade of grass.
Lu Xiaofeng could not for the life of him see what was worth looking at in that bare patch, and could not help asking, "Little cousin, what are you looking at?"
Xue'er neither spoke nor turned her head; not a pedant poring over the classics could have been more intent than she.
What in the world was the little imp looking at? Lu Xiaofeng's own curiosity was pricked despite himself.
So he too crouched down, at Xue'er's side. Where her eyes were fixed, there he fixed his own; and he saw nothing at all.

It had plainly not rained here in a long while; the earth was dry, and though the garden without was thick with flower and grass, here was only a stretch of yellow clay where not an inch of green would grow.

The well too seemed long unused; a film of yellow dust lay on the frame of its windlass. Along the two sides of the courtyard stood a few dilapidated side-rooms, the iron locks on their doors gone to rust.
Look as he might, Lu Xiaofeng could not make out what Xue'er was doing, crouched there.
Xue'er said of a sudden, "This was where my grandfather sat in meditation and studied Chan, when he was alive."
Lu Xiaofeng knew her grandfather for Shangguan Jin, who long ago had been charged, with Huo Xiu, to keep the orphaned prince: the Great King's own great-uncle of the royal house.
Xue'er said, "Since my grandfather died a year ago, no one has come here at all."
At last Lu Xiaofeng could not help asking again, "And what have you come here to do?"
Xue'er twisted her head round sharply and glared at him. "That's the very thing I want to ask you. What have you come here to do?"
"I, I came to find you," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Find me for what?" said Xue'er.
"To see how you were, and have a word with you," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Xue'er set her face and smiled coldly. "You don't believe a single word I say; what have I to talk to you about?"
Lu Xiaofeng smiled. "And how do you know I don't believe a single word you say?"
"You said so yourself," said Xue'er.
Lu Xiaofeng blinked. "And do you think every word I say is true?"
Xue'er glared at him out of her two great eyes, glared a long while, then laughed of a sudden.
Lu Xiaofeng laughed too, and found of a sudden that when Xue'er laughed she looked a truly sweet and biddable girl.
But Xue'er set her face again. "Whatever you want to talk of, then talk of it now."
"I wanted to ask you," said Lu Xiaofeng, "when you last saw your sister."
"The very day you brought Hua Manlou back," said Xue'er; "the same day we went out to find you."
"And after you came back, you never saw her again?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"No," said Xue'er.
Sorrow came over her face again. "She was always good to me; even when she went out, she'd tell me of it. But this time, this time she must have been murdered."
Lu Xiaofeng's eyes grew thoughtful. "Did she often go out, as a rule?"

"She never dared to, before," said Xue'er; "but after my grandfather died she grew bolder by degrees. Not only did she go out more and more, but often she'd be gone a full fortnight without coming back. I always suspected she had a lover somewhere; but she'd die before she'd own it."
She added, "Our mother and father died when we were small, and we were always in our grandfather's keeping; so she feared neither heaven nor earth, but she feared my grandfather."
"Did your uncle not keep her in check, later?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Xue'er shook her head. "He tried, and couldn't. Once he even locked her in her room, and still she found a way to slip out."
"Was he unkind to your sister, as a rule?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"He was. He was forever scolding her, saying she'd shamed the good name of the Shangguan house; and my sister paid him no mind at all."
She bit her lip, and said softly, "And it was for that reason I suspected it was he who had my sister killed."
"But your sister isn't dead," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Who says so?" said Xue'er.
"Hua Manlou saw her, not long since," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Xue'er smiled coldly. "He saw my sister? He's blind as a bat; how should he see my sister?"
"He knew the sound of your sister's voice," said Lu Xiaofeng.

Xue'er's face changed of a sudden. "Then it must have been Shangguan Danfeng, playing at being her. The two of them were somewhat alike to look at, and as children they'd often mimic each other's voices. Once she covered her face and aped my sister's voice to trick me, and even I was taken in."
A very strange look came over Lu Xiaofeng's face too; the affair grew stranger and stranger, and yet, at the same time, more and more diverting.
Xue'er clenched her fists hard, and said of a sudden, "Now that you put it so, I see it plainly. The one who killed my sister must be her."
"You mean Shangguan Danfeng?" said Lu Xiaofeng.

Xue'er nodded. "To all seeming she was good to my sister; but my sister always said it was hollow, every bit of it, for in her heart she was jealous that my sister was cleverer than she, and prettier too."
She would not let Lu Xiaofeng get a word in, but hurried on: "After she killed my sister, she played my sister's part before Hua Manlou on purpose, to make you all believe my sister still living."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed, and did not know what to say. Absurd as Xue'er's tale was, it was not wholly beyond the bounds of the possible.
Xue'er caught his hand of a sudden. "So you must do me a favour."
"What favour?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Help me dig up my sister's body!" said Xue'er.
"You know where your sister's body is buried?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I do," said Xue'er. "It must be right here."
Lu Xiaofeng wanted to laugh, and could not.
But Xue'er's face was grave. "I kept searching the garden, and so I never found it. Only now do I see: it must have been here she killed my sister, and here she buried the body."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "And how did you come to see that?"

"In his last years my grandfather grew like an old monk," said Xue'er; "he wouldn't so much as tread an ant to death, and would often scatter broken rice to feed them. So this courtyard used to be full of ants."
Her face had flushed with excitement. "But I've watched here two hours now, and I've not seen a single ant."
"And so you conclude—" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Xue'er cut in: "I conclude there's poison under this ground, so that even the ants dare not come."
"Poison?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"She must have poisoned my sister to death," said Xue'er; "and now the poison has seeped out of my sister's body into the soil, so that even the very earth here has been poisoned dead."
"Earth can be poisoned to death?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Of course it can," said Xue'er. "There are two kinds of earth, the living and the dead; only on living earth will flower and grass grow, and only there are there little insects and ants."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed again. "You think too much. A child who lets her fancies run wild will grow old the faster for it."
Xue'er glared at him. "You won't help me, then?"
Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly. "I've done fool's work enough for one day already."
Xue'er glared at him a while longer, then screamed out of a sudden, "Help! Help! Lu Xiaofeng means to ravish me!"
Lu Xiaofeng was in a fluster too. "I haven't so much as touched you; what are you shrieking about?"
Xue'er smiled coldly. "I'll not only scream it now; hereafter, whenever I meet anyone who knows you, I'll tell him you're forever ravishing me!"
Lu Xiaofeng cried out too. "I'm forever ravishing you?"
"Mm. 'Forever' meaning you've ravished me a great many, many times already," said Xue'er.
"You think anyone will believe a little chit's nonsense?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Anyone who won't believe it," said Xue'er, "I'll strip off my clothes and show him, and let him see whether I'm not still a child!"
Lu Xiaofeng stared at her, shaking his head without cease, and muttered, "The girl's mad. She must be mad!"
"Well, then, mad I'm, and so I'll go on screaming," said Xue'er; and scream again she truly did.
But this time Lu Xiaofeng clapped a hand over her mouth quickly. "You'd have me dig this very moment, is that it?"
Xue'er nodded; and the moment his hand came away she said at once, "Then you've agreed?"
Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly. "I only wonder who taught you a trick like that."
Xue'er laughed again. "It's one of the three oldest ways a woman has of handling a man; and only now do I find that it works after all."
"And what are the other two ways?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Xue'er smiled sweetly. "As if I'd tell you that! I'm keeping them to use on you; I can't have you learning them."
She sprang up. "I'll go for a hoe; wait here like a good boy. Tonight I'll steal a few pigeons and roast them to go with your wine."
"Pigeons?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"My sister kept a great many pigeons," said Xue'er. "She'd let no one so much as touch them; but now, now I think she'll not mind."
Sorrow came over her face again; of a sudden she turned and ran quickly off.
Lu Xiaofeng watched her two long braids swinging to and fro behind her, and a very strange look came into his eyes again; of a sudden he sprang up and caught her. "I'll come with you for the hoe."
"Why?" said Xue'er.
Lu Xiaofeng smiled. "I'm afraid the pigeons might carry you off." And there was something strange, it seemed, in his smile too.
Xue'er looked at him. "You're afraid I'll vanish all of a sudden, the way my sister did?"
A gust of cool wind passed; a few swallows rose from the flowers and flew away beyond the wall. The light was failing by degrees.
Lu Xiaofeng gazed after the swallows' shapes as they melted slowly into the dusk, and sighed of a sudden, long and deep. "Even the swallows won't stay here; how much less a living soul?"
Had Shangguan Feiyan too flown away, like these swallows? Or was she buried under the yellow clay?
And why had Shangguan Danfeng vanished as well? Did the Great King already know where she was, and was that why he had never once asked Lu Xiaofeng for word of her?
On those feet of his that had been cut away, had there been a sixth toe after all? Who knew the answers to such questions?
Dusk, and after dusk. The wind was colder and clearer now; and when the cold, clear wind blew in at the window and touched Hua Manlou, he knew that night had fallen.
His skin, like his nose and his ears, had a sense far keener than other men's.
But he had no heart now to savour the cool wind of that fourth-month dusk; his mind was in disorder.
Ever since he had met Shangguan Feiyan in that little shop, his mind would often fall into disorder, above all when he was quite alone.
He felt always that something was greatly amiss; yet what it was, he could not himself have said.
It was near the supper hour now; Lu Xiaofeng had not come back, and the Great King had sent no one to bid them make ready to sup.
Things seemed to have shifted once more; he could feel it even now; but what the change would be, that too he could not say.
Just then he caught of a sudden, on the wind, a strange fragrance again, the very fragrance that so troubled his heart.
Could Shangguan Feiyan have come back? He laid a hand light on the sill and was over it in a moment; he trusted his own senses never to be wrong.
But he could see nothing. In his world there was never light, never colour; only darkness, a darkness without hope.

The fragrance of a moment since seemed to have mingled with the scent of the flowers, so that he could no longer tell from which way it came; but of a sudden he heard a voice speak out of the place where the flower-scent was thickest: "I've come back." It was Shangguan Feiyan's voice indeed.
Hua Manlou mastered the stir in his heart as best he could, and after a long while sighed softly. "So you've come back."
"You knew I'd come back?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"I didn't know," said Hua Manlou. "I only hoped you would."
"You were thinking of me?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
Hua Manlou smiled, and in the smile was a feeling past telling, whether gladness or bitterness there was no knowing.
But Shangguan Feiyan had come to him and caught his hand. "I've come back; why are you not glad of it?"
"I, there is only one thing I can't work out," said Hua Manlou.
"What thing?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"These two times I've met you," said Hua Manlou, "I've thought each time of another."
"Thought of whom?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"Shangguan Danfeng," said Hua Manlou.
As he spoke the name, he felt Shangguan Feiyan's hand give a slight tremor.
But her hand tightened on his at once, and with a touch of pretty pique she said, "You meet me, and think of her instead?"
"Yes," said Hua Manlou.
"Why?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"Because, because at times I take you and her for one and the same person," said Hua Manlou.
Shangguan Feiyan laughed. "How should you come to feel such a thing?"
"I don't know myself," said Hua Manlou, "and so, so it often seems strange to me too."
"Have you too believed my little sister's tale, then," said Shangguan Feiyan, "that Shangguan Feiyan has been murdered, and that the Shangguan Feiyan here now is only Shangguan Danfeng in disguise?"
Hua Manlou did not speak; for in truth just such a doubt was in his heart, and he would not tell a lie before the one he loved.

"Do you remember Cui Yidong?" said Shangguan Feiyan. "Do you remember how once you asked me whether I had ever heard the sound of snowflakes settling on a roof? Whether I could feel that wondrous force of life in a flower-bud as it opens slowly in the spring wind? Whether I knew that the autumn wind often carries the clean scent of leaves, borne down from the far hills?"
Hua Manlou remembered, of course. These were his own words; and Shangguan Feiyan now spoke them back to him without a word amiss.
"Were I Shangguan Danfeng," said Shangguan Feiyan, "how should I know these words of yours? How should I remember them so clearly?"
Hua Manlou smiled; he found of a sudden that his doubt had been quite needless.
For this girl he felt, despite himself, a pang of contrition again; and he could not help reaching out a gentle hand to stroke her hair.

Shangguan Feiyan had sunk into his arms, and held him tight; and his heart knew only a happiness and a fullness past telling, so that he had all but forgotten everything. And it was then that he felt of a sudden Shangguan Feiyan's hand seal the Jade Pillow point at the back of his head; and after that he felt nothing at all.
In the ground now was a great pit, a good zhang across and two chi deep; and Lu Xiaofeng was in a lather of sweat.
Shangguan Xue'er crouched at his side, chin propped in both hands, urging him on without cease. "What are you stopping for? Dig on, quick! A great strong fellow like you, how can you be so useless?"

Lu Xiaofeng wiped the sweat with his sleeve, and smiled wryly. "Because I've had no supper. By rights I should be sitting in a comfortable chair this minute, drinking with your uncle; instead here I'm, digging a hole like a fool."
Xue'er blinked. "Would you've the face to set a little girl like me to dig, while you stood by and watched?"
"I wouldn't," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and that's just why I'm the one out of luck."
"How can it be ill luck?" said Xue'er. "It's an honour."
"An honour?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Why, another man might kneel on the ground and beg to dig for me, and I still wouldn't let him," said Xue'er.
Lu Xiaofeng sighed; he saw of a sudden that he ought never to have come to this little sprite at all, ought never to have said a word to her.
But at once he found that thought mistaken too. As his hoe bit down, he saw of a sudden a corner of bright-red cloth show through the earth.
Xue'er had sprung up. "There, you see I was right! Is there not someone buried down there?"
This time he needed no urging; Lu Xiaofeng too fell to it in earnest, set down the hoe and took up a spade, and after a few spadefuls the buried body came slowly to light, not yet gone to rot.
Xue'er had fetched over the lantern that hung by the well, and its light fell full on the dead face.
She gave a sudden cry, and could not hold the lantern steady; it near fell out of her hand onto Lu Xiaofeng.
Lu Xiaofeng too was struck dumb. Scarce ever in all his life had he been so astonished.
For the body was not Shangguan Feiyan at all. It was, past all doubt, Shangguan Danfeng.
The lantern-light swung ceaselessly to and fro, for Xue'er's hand would not stop shaking.
The dead face had not rotted at all; more, it kept the very colour of life, and the two great eyes, their pupils bulging out, seemed to be glaring at Lu Xiaofeng.

Lu Xiaofeng was no coward at any time; but thinking of the things Shangguan Danfeng had said to him not long before, of those sweet and stirring smiles of hers, his hand went weak, and he could no longer keep his grip on the spade.

As the spade fell from his hand, it chanced to strike the body; and there came a "clang," for all the world like iron on iron. Lu Xiaofeng could not help reaching out to feel it, and found the body hard and cold, hard as very steel.
His hand went cold too; he could not help a long sigh. "So she was poisoned after all."
"Who, who poisoned her?" said Xue'er.
Lu Xiaofeng did not answer; he had no answer at all.
"A poisoned corpse rots quickly, as a rule," said Xue'er; "it seems she wasn't poisoned so very long ago."
"It was long ago," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"How do you know?" said Xue'er.
"Because the poison in her body has seeped out already, into the soil," said Lu Xiaofeng.
This was Xue'er's own saying, and in it she had not been wrong after all.
"And more," said Lu Xiaofeng, "by the look of this ground, it hasn't been turned in a month or two at the least."
"You mean she has been dead a month or two at the least," said Xue'er.
"Just so," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Then why has her body not rotted?" said Xue'er.

"Because the poison she took was a strange one," said Lu Xiaofeng. "There are drugs that'll keep a corpse whole for hundreds of years; and besides, this ground is dry, and clean of insect and ant. Whoever's body were buried here would be slow to rot."
His voice was flat and slow, for while his mouth was speaking his mind was on other things. He had far, far too much to think about.
Xue'er too was musing, and murmured, "A month or two ago, my sister hadn't yet gone to Hua Manlou."
Lu Xiaofeng, deep in thought, nodded.
"It was after my sister brought Hua Manlou back that I went with them to find you," said Xue'er.
"Just so," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"If she was dead a month or two ago," said Xue'er, "how could she have gone to you? How could you've seen her?"
"The Shangguan Danfeng I saw," said Lu Xiaofeng, "wasn't the true Shangguan Danfeng."
"Then who was it?" said Xue'er.
Lu Xiaofeng did not answer, but asked in his turn, "These two months past, have you ever seen your sister and her appear at one and the same time?"
Xue'er thought a long while, then shook her head. "I think not."
"And these two months," said Lu Xiaofeng, "have you felt there was something strange in the way she treated you?"
Xue'er thought a long while again, then nodded. "I think there was. Before, when we met, she'd talk and laugh with me; but of late she seemed always to be avoiding me."
"That is only because she was no longer the true Shangguan Danfeng," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and feared you would see through her."
Xue'er knit her brows. "Then who could she be? To play the part so close, could it be—"
She sprang up again of a sudden, and cried aloud, "Do you mean the Shangguan Danfeng you saw was my sister in disguise?"
Lu Xiaofeng said nothing; and to say nothing is, at times, as good as to own it.
Xue'er stared. "Do you mean that Shangguan Danfeng never killed my sister at all, but that my sister killed her?"
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "I know only that she is dead now, past doubt."
"Why should my sister want to kill her?" said Xue'er. "Can you give me a reason?"
Lu Xiaofeng did not say; whether he could not or would not, there was no telling. Of a sudden he crouched down and began to draw off the dead woman's shoes.
Xue'er cried out despite herself, "What are you about?"
"I want to see her feet," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Xue'er cried out, "You're mad! You're a madman through and through!"
Lu Xiaofeng sighed, and smiled wryly. "I know well enough there's a touch of madness in it; but see them I must."
He had drawn the shoes off; and on a pair of slender, delicate feet there were, past all doubt, six toes indeed.
Xue'er fell suddenly still, and after a long while said, low and sorrowful, "It really is my cousin."
"You knew, then, that your cousin had six toes?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Yes," said Xue'er.
"How did you know?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"She, she would never let anyone see her feet," said Xue'er. "Sometimes we'd all take off our shoes and go to play in the river, and she alone wouldn't."
Girls are all vain of their looks, and six toes on a foot are no thing to be proud of.
"The less she would let anyone look, the more I wanted to," said Xue'er; "and so, one day, while she was bathing, I burst in on her all at once."
Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly, and could only smile wryly; there seemed to be nothing this little sprite would not do.
"When she saw me she was angry at first," said Xue'er, "and then she begged me not to tell anyone of it."
"And you promised?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Xue'er nodded. "I never told a soul!"
"And your sister?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"She didn't know either; I never told her," said Xue'er.
Lu Xiaofeng pondered, then asked of a sudden, "When were your uncle's feet cut off?"
Surprise showed in Xue'er's face. "His feet, cut off? How is it I never knew?"
Lu Xiaofeng's face changed. "You truly didn't know?"
"Only yesterday at noon I saw him walking to and fro where my sister keeps her pigeons," said Xue'er, "as though he were feeding them for her."
A light came of a sudden into Lu Xiaofeng's eyes.
"These two months," said Xue'er, "if someone has truly been playing at being my cousin, how is it that even my uncle never saw through it?"
She meant to ask it of Lu Xiaofeng; but by now Lu Xiaofeng had of a sudden vanished.
The night was bleak and cold; the dim lantern-light fell on the corpse's ice-cold face, and the two empty, hollow eyes seemed again to be glaring at her.
Xue'er could not help a shiver running through her; and of a sudden she heard a voice say coldly, out of the dark, "You shouldn't have meddled."
She knew the voice, and her heart sank in her.
The corridor was grim and dark, and the door was shut. Lu Xiaofeng knocked; there was no answer. He knocked harder; still no answer.
His face had changed. Of a sudden he threw his weight against it, and the wooden door, a good three cun thick, burst into flying splinters under him.
The brass lamp on the table was lit, but the chair stood empty; here the Great King of the Golden Roc was ever wont to sit, and now he was gone.
Yet Lu Xiaofeng showed no surprise; the change seemed to be one he had looked for all along.
The coverlet worked with golden dragons had fallen from the couch to the floor; he bent to take it up, and saw of a sudden a hand.
A withered, shrunken hand, thrust out from behind the chair, its five fingers crooked, as though it had reached to seize something and seized nothing.
Lu Xiaofeng went over, and there he saw the Great King of the Golden Roc.

The old man's body was not yet gone quite cold and stiff, but his breath had long since stopped; and in his eyes was a terror and a wrath past all describing, for plainly, to his last breath, he had not believed the one who killed him could truly bring himself to strike.
On his other arm was a deep sword-gash, as though someone had meant to cut the hand away and had not cut it through.
His hand was clenched fast, the veins standing out on its back; plainly he would not, even in death, let go of the thing he gripped.
Lu Xiaofeng crouched down, and found that what the hand gripped was a bright-red embroidered shoe.
It was such a red embroidered shoe as a bride might wear; but what was worked upon it was neither a pair of mandarin ducks nor an owl, but a swallow—a swallow in flight.
He had gripped it so hard, with such force, that the once-pretty red shoe was now twisted quite out of shape.
But his face was wholly without expression; set against those bulging eyes, so full of terror and of rage, it looked the more dreadful and uncanny past telling.
Lu Xiaofeng had no need to touch it to see that the face had been very cunningly disguised.
This old man, plainly, was no true Great King of the Golden Roc either; and the true Great King had died, of course, at the same hour as his daughter.
Lu Xiaofeng looked into his eyes, and at his severed legs, and could not help a long sigh. "I've done my share of foolish things," he murmured; "but wasn't what you did more foolish still?"
He did not finish the words, for he had heard already a thin, keen whistle of a sword cleaving the air.

The sword-wind came thrusting in at the window behind him, swift and sudden; the man who struck at him from without was past doubt a first-rate swordsman of the martial world. First-rate swordsmen of the martial world are not many.
Lu Xiaofeng sighed; he knew already who the man was.
He slid his body three chi aside, and said with a sigh, "Liu Yuhen, you shouldn't have come just now."
And from beyond the window came Liu Yuhen's voice indeed, cold as ice: "But come I've."
His sword was quicker than his voice. The old, graceful carved window-lattice burst apart with a crash, and the man and the sword flew in together.
His hair hung loose, and in his eyes was a wild, feverish light; the man was far more fearful to look on than his sword.
Lu Xiaofeng did not look at the man.
The sword-light was fierce and swift, its strokes changing very fast, and every thrust went for a vital spot that would kill on the instant.
Lu Xiaofeng's eyes stayed fixed all the while on the sword's point, as a child watches a fluttering butterfly.
In the blink of an eye Liu Yuhen had thrust seventeen strokes more; and at that instant Lu Xiaofeng made his move.
He put out but two fingers and closed them; no one could tell the swiftness and the deftness of that motion, no one could so much as imagine it.
Heart and finger were of one mind—his fingers seemed now to do whatever his will bade them.
As Liu Yuhen thrust his eighteenth stroke, he found of a sudden that his sword's point was caught fast.
It was as though the stroke had driven of a sudden into a block of stone; strain with all his strength as he might, he could not draw it out.
The sword was fixed to his right wrist, part of his very body now; yet he could no more pull it free from between Lu Xiaofeng's fingers than he could let it go.

On that wrist he wore, at ordinary times, an iron hook, a hook for lifting all manner of things; only when he meant to kill was the hook changed for a sword. Plainly he had made ready to kill, and long since.
Lu Xiaofeng looked at the face, twisted now with pain, and a pity past telling rose of a sudden in his heart. "I've no wish to kill you," he said. "Go."
Liu Yuhen said nothing; his answer was the iron ball on his left wrist.
The iron ball came crashing down at Lu Xiaofeng with a rush of wind; and had Lu Xiaofeng not let go, his good head would have been beaten flat.
But he had another hand; and as the ball came down, that hand cut across it at a slant, and Liu Yuhen's left arm dropped useless to his side.
Lu Xiaofeng said slowly, "If I let go, will you go?"
Liu Yuhen laughed coldly of a sudden, and the laugh was full of scorn—scorn for Lu Xiaofeng, and scorn for his own life.
Lu Xiaofeng sighed, and smiled wryly. "Why must I forever meet with such foolish men? Why—"
He did not finish the words, for at that moment he heard a voice speak.
It was the voice of Shangguan Danfeng; but he knew now that Shangguan Danfeng would never appear again.
The last glow of the setting sun had gone, and the room was darker. A figure appeared of a sudden in the doorway, like a ghost: a woman of great beauty, beautiful with a soft and honeyed beauty.
She gazed at Lu Xiaofeng, and said with a smile, "Because you're a foolish man yourself; and fools are forever running into one another."
Lu Xiaofeng had never seen the woman before, but he knew already who she was. "Shangguan Feiyan?"
"Yes." She smiled like an innocent young girl. "Would you not say I'm prettier than Shangguan Danfeng?"
Lu Xiaofeng nodded; he could not but own it.
Shangguan Danfeng had been a woman of great beauty, past doubt; but the girl he saw before him now was beautiful near to the very dream that lives in every man's heart.

She was not only beautiful but pure and innocent with it; and when she looked at you, it was as though she had made you the one man in all the world to her, and made you feel, at the same moment, that she was the one woman.
Shangguan Danfeng's smile could set a man to dreaming; but this girl's smile could make him forget everything.
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "You're wrong."
"Wrong?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"A woman as lovely as you," said Lu Xiaofeng, "should never, for anything on earth, have played at being another."
Shangguan Feiyan blinked. "Had you seen my true face that night, would you still have let me go?"
"Had you shown me your true face sooner," said Lu Xiaofeng, "I might not have waited for that night at all."
"You mean, in the carriage, you'd have—" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"I've said it before," said Lu Xiaofeng: "I'm a man who can't hold out against temptation."
Shangguan Feiyan laughed. "No gentleman, you; but there's an honest tongue in your head."
"And you," said Lu Xiaofeng, "are no lady, and there's no honest word in yours."
Shangguan Feiyan smiled sweetly. "A girl too honest is bound to be taken in by a man like you."
The very sound of her voice had changed, so that it seemed some other person altogether was speaking now.
To Lu Xiaofeng, this sudden change of voice was a thing more marvellous even than the changing of a face.
He could understand the art of disguise; he had seen those masks of human skin that legend had made near to myth.
But he could not understand how one person's voice could be changed into another's.
Shangguan Feiyan had marked the wonder in his face, of course, and smiled. "Is my voice not sweeter, too, than Shangguan Danfeng's?"
Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly.
Shangguan Feiyan said, "By now you'll surely see that I'm the better of her in every way; and yet from the hour of my birth she was set above me."
Her soft, honeyed voice was of a sudden full of rancour. "From a child I wore the clothes she had outworn, and ate what she left on her plate, and only because she was the princess."
"And so, given the chance," said Lu Xiaofeng, "you meant to prove yourself the better of her."
Shangguan Feiyan smiled coldly.
"And so, the moment your grandfather died," said Lu Xiaofeng, "you'd stay at home no longer."
"No one likes to live beneath another's roof, and watch another's face for its temper," said Shangguan Feiyan.

"At first you meant only to make your own way in the jianghu by your own skill," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and do some few things to hold your head high before them; but you never thought that in the jianghu you'd meet a man to lose your heart to."
Shangguan Feiyan's face changed a little. "I knew long since that the little imp had told you everything."
"This man was greatly taken with you in his turn," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and pitied your lot besides; and so he found a chance to right your wrongs for you."
Shangguan Feiyan said coldly, "Go on."
"Once he knew the secret of the Golden Roc," said Lu Xiaofeng, "he laid a plan for you."
Shangguan Feiyan listened; the honeyed smile was gone from her face now.
"He urged you to find a way to win back the Golden Roc's fortune from Yan Tieshan and the rest," said Lu Xiaofeng; "for whoever held that vast fortune could rise above all men at a stroke."
"I'd not have another sit back and reap it, to be sure," said Shangguan Feiyan.
"And so you and your lover laid a fine scheme between you," said Lu Xiaofeng.

"At first I meant only to kill that old, doting Great King of the Golden Roc," said Shangguan Feiyan; "but the man we set to counterfeit him, however cunning the disguise, could never have got it past Shangguan Danfeng."
"And so you killed her too, and had done," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Just so," said Shangguan Feiyan.

"As it fell out," said Lu Xiaofeng, "your faces were somewhat alike to begin with, and you had aped her voice since childhood; so you could take her place, and taste for yourself what it was to be a princess."
Shangguan Feiyan smiled coldly. "The taste of it wasn't good."

"A secret of that kind you'd not have a chattering child know, of course," said Lu Xiaofeng; "and so you kept it from Xue'er all along. The laughable thing is that she took it, instead, that you had died at Shangguan Danfeng's hand."
Shangguan Feiyan said with venom, "The little imp isn't only a chatterer, but a meddler."
"I only wonder," said Lu Xiaofeng, "why you didn't go straight to Huo Xiu and the others."

"Because only afterward did we find that the Great King must bear some secret mark," said Shangguan Feiyan, "known only to the ministers who went into exile with him; so that whoever counterfeited him was bound to be seen through by those old foxes, Huo Xiu and the rest."
"You didn't yet know then that he was a man with six toes?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I didn't," said Shangguan Feiyan, "and I dared not chance it."
"And so you judged the best way was to find someone first to kill those old foxes off for you," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Just so," said Shangguan Feiyan.

Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly. "But such a man was none too easy to find; for he mustn't only have the skill to kill men like Huo Xiu, but the cursed born temper of one who loves to meddle in what is no affair of his."
"Such a man was hard to find indeed," said Shangguan Feiyan lightly; "save for you, we couldn't think of a second soul."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed, and smiled wryly. "It seems there are truly none too many men like me in the world."
"Only, to make you lift a hand of your own free will was no easy matter either," said Shangguan Feiyan.
"As luck would have it," said Lu Xiaofeng, "I not only love to meddle, but have something of the mule's temper: pull me and I balk, drive me and I back away."
Shangguan Feiyan smiled at last. "I'd not have thought you knew yourself so well."
"You set Soul-Hook and the rest to bar my way on purpose," said Lu Xiaofeng, "for you knew that the more a man forbids me a thing, the more I'll do it in his teeth."
Shangguan Feiyan laughed. "The mules of Shanxi are of the same mind."
"And later you killed Xiao Qiuyu and Dugu Fang to warn me off, which came to the same thing," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"That was because they had come to know too much, as well," said Shangguan Feiyan.
"In that ruined temple you lured us with a song on purpose, and left a few hairs in the water-basin on purpose, only to make Hua Manlou believe you still living, was it not?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"That too was to keep you from ever again believing the little imp's words," said Shangguan Feiyan.
"Knowing Xue'er was spying at the window, you 'killed' Liu Yuhen before her eyes on purpose," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Shangguan Feiyan said coldly, "The little imp couldn't know, of course, that it was only a play Liu Yuhen and I staged for her to see."

"And when we saw Liu Yuhen alive, of course we thought her the greater liar for it," said Lu Xiaofeng. He sighed again, and smiled wryly. "The pity of it: when she saw Liu Yuhen appear alive again, her face was as though she'd met a living ghost, and she dared not say a word, but went off with him meek as a lamb."
"I ought to have locked the little imp up long before," said Shangguan Feiyan; "but the pity was—"
"But the pity was that those few days you had too much to do," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and feared, besides, that if we came back and didn't see her, we'd only grow the more suspicious."
Shangguan Feiyan smiled coldly. "At times I could almost think you the worm in my own belly; you seem to know my every secret thought."
"You showed yourself before Hua Manlou once more on purpose," said Lu Xiaofeng, "meaning, of course, to lay the blame on Huo Xiu."
"Just so," said Shangguan Feiyan.
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "I only wonder how you got it past him; his ears are keen, and his nose keener, and even if he couldn't tell your voice, he should have caught your scent."
Every person has about them a breath unlike another's, easier to tell, even, than the sound of a voice.

"That was only because each time I met him I had sprinkled myself on purpose with a strong, heady flower-powder," said Shangguan Feiyan; "and when I came before him again as Shangguan Danfeng, I had washed the scent quite away."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "It seems you thought of everything."
Shangguan Feiyan smiled sweetly. "I'm a woman; and women are loath to take chances."
"Then why did you send Liu Yuhen to kill me?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Shangguan Feiyan said easily, "That reason you should know for yourself."
"Is it that he was no more use to you," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and so you'd have my hand kill him for you?"
Shangguan Feiyan sighed. "In truth I should have seen sooner that you've no taste for killing; else I'd not have had to see to Yan Tieshan myself."
From the moment she appeared, Liu Yuhen had been like another man, gone very still.
Whenever he looked at her, a look of the greatest tenderness would come into his one eye.
These words of Shangguan Feiyan's went like a sharp knife of a sudden into his heart. He said, his voice trembling, "You, you truly want me dead?"
Shangguan Feiyan did not so much as glance at him. "In truth you should have died long ago," she said coldly. "What meaning is there in the living, for a man like you?"
"But you, you, before—" said Liu Yuhen.
"The things I said to you before were all to deceive you, of course," said Shangguan Feiyan. "Did you truly think I could care for you?"

Liu Yuhen seemed frozen cold and stiff through all his body; he stood without a stir, gazing at her like a man bewitched, his one eye full of venom and yet full of love. How long passed there was no knowing; then he sighed, softly. "Just so. You could never truly care for me; I knew it myself. I've only been deceiving myself all this while."
"You're not altogether a fool, at least," said Shangguan Feiyan.
Liu Yuhen nodded slowly, then of a sudden turned the sword back on himself and drove it into his own breast.
The point went clean through his heart, and the blood spurted from his back like an arrow, spattering little by little against the wall.
Yet his face had gone wholly without expression again; to him, it seemed, death was no longer a thing of pain, but a thing to be savoured.
A light came of a sudden into his eyes; of a sudden he smiled, and murmured, "So dying is no hard thing after all. To die before you, I've at least—" He did not finish the words; he had fallen.
Lu Xiaofeng did not stay him, nor had he time to. For a man to die in peace is, at times, truly better than to live.

"Love, from of old, leaves only regret behind; he was a man of deep feeling in truth, only he gave his feeling amiss." Gazing at Shangguan Feiyan, Lu Xiaofeng felt of a sudden, for this heartless woman, a loathing past telling.
Not hatred, but loathing; the very feeling men have for a venomous snake.
He said coldly, "You too have done a foolish thing."
"Oh?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"You shouldn't have driven him to his death," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Why?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"Had he lived," said Lu Xiaofeng, "he'd not have stood by, at least, and watched me kill you."
"You'd kill me? You could bring yourself to kill me?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"It's true I've no wish to kill," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and I've never killed a woman; but you're the exception."
Shangguan Feiyan smiled. "In that case, why do you not strike?"
"I'm in no hurry," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Shangguan Feiyan smiled sweetly. "No hurry indeed; I can't run now in any case, and besides, you've surely more to ask me yet."
"You're no fool either," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"You'd ask me, would you," said Shangguan Feiyan, "how it was that, before you got here, I had Liu Yuhen cut off the old man's feet? How I came suddenly to know that he should have six toes?"
"That I needn't ask," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"You know already?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"A pigeon flies faster than a man, to be sure," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Shangguan Feiyan sighed. "You're a clever man indeed."
"I ought never to have let the secret slip to Ye Xiuzhu," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"You told her alone?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"Just so," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Did you let it slip unmeaning?" said Shangguan Feiyan. "Or were you sounding her on purpose?"
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "I meant her no harm; she too is a soul to be pitied."
Shangguan Feiyan smiled coldly of a sudden. "You've misjudged her. Honest as the woman looks, she is a born whore."
"Only because she loves the same man as you?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Shangguan Feiyan's face went livid. "He is only using her, as I used Liu Yuhen, no more."
"Ye Xiuzhu told him the secret," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and he sent word to you by carrier-pigeon."
Shangguan Feiyan nodded, and a tenderness came over her face again of a sudden. "Those black pigeons we kept for carrying love-letters; I'd not have thought they'd come to serve another turn."
"Since he commands Soul-Hook and the Iron-Faced Judge to do his work," said Lu Xiaofeng, "can it be that he is the head of the Blue-Robe Tower?"
"What do you think?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"I can't tell," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Do you think I'd tell you?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"You'll not tell me now, of course," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Nor will I tell you hereafter," said Shangguan Feiyan. "You'll never know who he is."
"But you're a woman," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"And what of it, that I'm a woman?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
Lu Xiaofeng said coldly, "A woman as lovely as you, were her nose cut off, would turn very ugly indeed."
Shangguan Feiyan cried out despite herself, "You, you could bring yourself to cut off my nose?"
"If you think my heart softer than bean-curd," said Lu Xiaofeng lightly, "you're wrong."
Shangguan Feiyan stared at him in alarm. "If I won't tell you who he is, you'll cut off my nose?"
"The nose first," said Lu Xiaofeng, "then the ears."
Shangguan Feiyan smiled sweetly. "Fierce words in your mouth; but I know well enough you could never truly do such a thing."
Lu Xiaofeng's face darkened. "Care to try me?"
"I know you'll not so much as try," said Shangguan Feiyan, "for you'd never care for a friend with no nose."
"As well, then, that you're no friend of mine," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I'm not," said Shangguan Feiyan; "but Hua Manlou and Zhu Ting are."
Lu Xiaofeng's face changed too.
Shangguan Feiyan said easily, "Cut off my nose, and I fear they'll not keep their heads; and is a man without a head not a shade uglier than a woman without a nose?"
Lu Xiaofeng stared at her, then laughed aloud of a sudden.
"You think it a laughing matter?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
Lu Xiaofeng laughed. "You'd have me believe you've deceived Hua Manlou again?"
"If I could deceive him once, I can deceive him a second time," said Shangguan Feiyan.
"Only a fool is deceived twice," said Lu Xiaofeng. "He is no fool."
"But he is a man of deep feeling," said Shangguan Feiyan; "a fool is taken in twice at the most, but a man of feeling may be deceived two hundred times, for it is his own heart's willing choice."
"And is Zhu Ting a man of deep feeling too?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"He isn't," said Shangguan Feiyan. "He is too lazy."
"There's a virtue in a lazy man," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Oh?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"He's too lazy even to stir," said Lu Xiaofeng; "how should he ever be taken in by anyone?"
Shangguan Feiyan smiled. "To take in a man as lazy as that is no easy thing indeed; as luck would have it, he has a good friend who sent him a banknote, and so brought him to be taken in."
Lu Xiaofeng could laugh no longer.
Shangguan Feiyan said of a sudden, "You'd not stand by, of course, and watch him lose his head for the sake of a good friend like you; the more so with a bewitching Boss's Wife to die at his side!"
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "The Boss's Wife is lazier, as a rule, than the Boss himself; how comes she to be here this time?"
"Because she knows you're sure to come and save her," said Shangguan Feiyan. "She is waiting for you."
"And where does she wait for me?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"You'd like to know?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"Very much," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Do you think I'll take you there?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"You won't," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"You're wrong," said Shangguan Feiyan. "If I wouldn't take you, why should I've told you at all?"
"At least you'll not take me there now," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Shangguan Feiyan smiled sweetly. "You're a clever man indeed."
Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly. "The pity is that my friends are either too lazy or too foolish."
"But your friends they're, when all's said," said Shangguan Feiyan; "and go to save them you'll, of course."
"I can think it over," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Think what over?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"I must first see what it is you'd have me do," said Lu Xiaofeng, "before you'll take me there."
"What I'd have you do," said Shangguan Feiyan, "is but a very easy thing, I think."
"What thing?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I'd only have you kill a man for me," said Shangguan Feiyan; "and killing, for you, is surely an easy thing?"
"That depends on whom you'd have me kill," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"This is a man you can surely deal with," said Shangguan Feiyan.
"Who?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Ximen Chuixue," said Shangguan Feiyan.
Lu Xiaofeng laughed. "Is it that you'd have me kill him? Or that you'd have him kill me?"
"That you should kill him, to be sure," said Shangguan Feiyan. "He insulted me; no one has ever insulted me as he did."
"And for that alone you'd have him dead?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"A woman's heart is a narrow thing, always," said Shangguan Feiyan.
"And if I fail to kill him, and he kills me instead?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Then you needn't grieve," said Shangguan Feiyan; "on the road to the Yellow Springs you'll have friends enough hastening to keep you company."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "It seems I've little room left to choose."
"None at all," said Shangguan Feiyan.
"Whether he dies or I die," said Lu Xiaofeng, "you'll be well pleased either way."
"In honest truth," said Shangguan Feiyan, "were the two of you both to die, I'd not grieve."
"I'd not have thought you had a conscience at all!" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Of course I've," said Shangguan Feiyan. "And so I'd have you kill him, and trade his one life for the three lives of Hua Manlou and the rest."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "The reckoning's no bad bargain; the pity is I don't know where he is."
"You can surely find him," said Shangguan Feiyan.
"And how am I to find him?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"That day he carried off Sun Xiuqing," said Shangguan Feiyan, "and to save Sun Xiuqing's life, to be sure."
"Beyond killing men, he'll now and then save one," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"So he must be now in some place where Sun Xiuqing can mend of her wound; and what place there is thereabouts for the mending of wounds, you should know," said Shangguan Feiyan.
"But the dead have no need to mend," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Just so," said Shangguan Feiyan.
"So this too I must ask of you," said Lu Xiaofeng: "after Sun Xiuqing was struck by your Flying Phoenix Needles, was she past saving?"

Shangguan Feiyan said coldly, "What struck her wasn't the Flying Phoenix Needles, but a Flying Swallow Needle; and past saving she should have been, only Ximen Chuixue seems to be no small adept himself."
"Oh?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"The poison of the Flying Swallow Needle is unlike that of common hidden weapons," said Shangguan Feiyan. "Once struck by it, lie still and quiet, and you die past all doubt."
"And so Shi Xiuxue is dead," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"But Ximen Chuixue carried Sun Xiuqing at a run over the whole mountain," said Shangguan Feiyan, "and so drove the poison out of her; and so she may yet be saved."
"That day, after you struck her down," said Lu Xiaofeng, "you didn't leave?"
Shangguan Feiyan smiled. "Before adepts like you, how could I get away? So I hid myself there instead; and while you went out to chase me, I watched the whole time."
Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly. "You're bold enough, and no mistake."
"I knew you'd never think I'd dare stay there," said Shangguan Feiyan.
"And once we'd all gone, you came out?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"By then only Hua Manlou was left," said Shangguan Feiyan. "I knew he'd never suspect me; I might have told him snow was black and ink was white, and still he'd have believed me."
"Why?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Shangguan Feiyan smiled sweetly. "Because he loves me; and when a man loves a woman, there is truly no help for it."
"And because he loves you," said Lu Xiaofeng, "you hold that he deserves to be cheated and undone?"
"That is his own heart's willing choice," said Shangguan Feiyan. "I never asked him to love me."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed of a sudden again. "There is only one thing left for me to tell you now."
"Say it," said Shangguan Feiyan.
"A man who takes everyone else for a fool," said Lu Xiaofeng, "is himself the first great fool under heaven."
Shangguan Feiyan frowned. "What do you mean by that?"
"Turn and look behind you," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and you'll take my meaning."
Shangguan Feiyan turned her head; and she felt as though her whole self had of a sudden dropped into a deep, black pit.
The room was darker now; a figure stood silent in the dark, without a stir.
"Hua Manlou!" Shangguan Feiyan cried out at last, despite herself.
But Hua Manlou's face was very calm; there was in it no least trace of pain or anger.
Shangguan Feiyan looked at him, and said in astonishment, "You, how did you come to be here?"
"I walked here," said Hua Manlou lightly.
"But I, I sealed your points, plainly I did!" said Shangguan Feiyan.

"When another seals your points," said Hua Manlou, "if you can drive your true breath to the place about them, then after a while you may find a way to burst the sealed point open again; and this art I happen to know a little of."
"Did you foresee, then, that I would strike?" said Shangguan Feiyan. "Were you ready for it all along?"
"I didn't want a friend of mine to kill for the sake of saving me," said Hua Manlou.
"And all I said just now, you heard it too?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
Hua Manlou nodded.
"You, you, you're not angry?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"Every one of us must sometimes do wrong," said Hua Manlou lightly; "and besides, you never did ask me to love you."
He looked as calm, as gentle, as ever; for in his heart there was only love, and no hate.
Shangguan Feiyan looked at him; and even in a woman such as she, a look of shame could not be kept from the face.
Lu Xiaofeng too was watching him, and sighed softly. "Here is a true gentleman indeed."
Hua Manlou smiled. "A gentleman and a fool are much of a muchness, at times."
"And the Boss?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"The Boss is keeping the Boss's Wife company, of course," said Hua Manlou.
"Why don't they come?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"They're listening to Xue'er tell a story," said Hua Manlou.
Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly. "It seems their turn to be taken in is near at hand too."
In truth he knew well enough why they did not come. It was for his sake they had been deceived; and meeting them, he could not but feel some shame, and they had no wish to make him feel it.
And Xue'er had no wish to see her sister either; meeting, in such a case, would sit ill with them both.
Shangguan Feiyan sighed at last, long and deep. "The thing you said just now, I take its meaning now at last."
"Oh?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"It seems it is I who have done the truly foolish thing," said Shangguan Feiyan, "foolish past all cure."
"Oh?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"All this while I took you all for fools," said Shangguan Feiyan; "and only now do I see that the real fool was myself."
She sighed again. "But even were you truly to cut off my nose, I wouldn't tell you who he is."
"So you too are one of deep feeling, after all," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Shangguan Feiyan smiled, a smile of great desolation. "When a woman loves a man, there is no help for that either."
Hua Manlou nodded slowly. "I understand. I understand."
Shangguan Feiyan said, low and sorrowful, "Only, I've wronged you truly; and were you to kill me, I'd hold it no blame in you."
"I've no wish to harm you," said Hua Manlou.
"What would you do with me, then?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"Nothing at all," said Hua Manlou.
Shangguan Feiyan's face moved. "You, you'd truly let me go?"
Hua Manlou said nothing at all; of a sudden he turned and walked slowly out. Lu Xiaofeng sighed, and, for a wonder, walked out after him.
Shangguan Feiyan stared at them in alarm, then cried aloud of a sudden, "I take your meaning now: you know I'll go straight to him, and so you let me go on purpose, to follow me from behind."
Lu Xiaofeng did not turn his head. "I've no need to do that," he said lightly.
"Why?" said Shangguan Feiyan.
"Because I know already who he is," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Shangguan Feiyan's colour changed, and she cried aloud, "You know who he is? Who is he?"
Lu Xiaofeng did not answer, and said no more; he caught up with Hua Manlou, and side by side they passed down the shadowed corridor, and out into the dark.
The room, too, was all in darkness.
Shangguan Feiyan stood alone in the dark, and of a sudden her body began to shake, whether from the cold or from fear there was no telling.
The garden was dark and still; the flower-scent on the wind seemed heavier even than before dusk, and a few dozen faint autumn stars had just risen, only to be veiled again by a thin drift of cloud.
Hua Manlou walked very slowly; and coming to a clump of China roses he sighed softly at last. "She too is a girl to be pitied."
Lu Xiaofeng nodded, as though he had forgotten that Hua Manlou could not see him nod.
"Every one of us must sometimes do wrong," said Hua Manlou. "She has done wrong, it's true; and yet—"
Lu Xiaofeng cut him short. "Who does wrong must be punished for it; whoever does wrong must pay the price."
"But you let her go," said Hua Manlou.
"That may be only because I know there is one who won't let her go," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Who? Her lover?" said Hua Manlou.
"No lover," said Lu Xiaofeng. "He is a man without feeling."
"Do you truly know who he is?" said Hua Manlou.
"Not truly," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Was she wrong, then?" said Hua Manlou. "Did you mean to follow her in secret?"
Lu Xiaofeng smiled. "No gentleman, I; but not so far gone as to go back on my word."
"If you don't know who the man is, and won't follow her," said Hua Manlou, "do you mean to let the matter rest, then?"
"It won't rest," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I don't take your meaning," said Hua Manlou.
"I can't find the man," said Lu Xiaofeng, "but he is sure to come and find me."
"You're certain of it?" said Hua Manlou.
"Seven parts certain, at the least," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Oh?" said Hua Manlou.
"By now he must believe I know who he is," said Lu Xiaofeng; "how should he suffer me to live?"
"You said what you did just now on purpose, then," said Hua Manlou, "to make him come to you?"
"Saying it," said Lu Xiaofeng, "was as good as saving Shangguan Feiyan, too."
"Since you know who he is," said Hua Manlou, "he needn't kill Shangguan Feiyan now to stop her mouth."
Lu Xiaofeng smiled again. "At least the first he'll want to kill now is me, and not Shangguan Feiyan."
"The pity is he didn't hear what you said just now," said Hua Manlou.
"He heard it," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Hua Manlou frowned. "Do you mean he was there just now as well?"
"He is surely there still," said Lu Xiaofeng.
