"So he may appear at any moment," said Hua Manlou, "and at any moment take your life."
"Just so," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Yet you seem not the least troubled by it," said Hua Manlou.
Lu Xiaofeng smiled. "The best thing about me is just this—"
He had not finished the words when he found of a sudden that Hua Manlou's face had changed. Hua Manlou was not a man whose colour changed easily.
Lu Xiaofeng could not help asking, "What is it?"
"Blood," said Hua Manlou, low.
"What blood? Whose blood?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I only hope it isn't Shangguan Feiyan's—" said Hua Manlou.

The blood was Shangguan Feiyan's. Her throat had been cut, and the blood was not yet clotted. Her face was full of shock and terror, the very look the Great King of the Golden Roc had worn as he died. Plainly she too had never thought that the one who killed her could truly bring himself to strike; even in death she did not believe it.
Her lover? Or the man without feeling? No one was there; only darkness.
The reek of blood on the wind was heavy still. Hua Manlou said, low and grieving, "He killed her, after all."
"Yes," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Plainly he didn't believe what you said," said Hua Manlou.
"Yes," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Now that he has killed Shangguan Feiyan to stop her mouth," said Hua Manlou, "there may not be a second soul in the world who knows who he is."
"Yes," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"And so you'll never find him," said Hua Manlou.
Lu Xiaofeng said of a sudden, "I know only that whoever does wrong must surely pay the price."
Hua Manlou said, low and sorrowful, "Shangguan Feiyan has paid her price indeed; but what of the man who killed her?"
The man who had killed her had vanished into the dark, vanished, perhaps, for good.
Lu Xiaofeng caught Hua Manlou's hand of a sudden. "And the Boss?"
The Boss was gone; the cellar where they had been penned held no one now. An old rosewood table lay overturned on the floor, and the teapot and cups upon it were smashed to bits.
"They must have crossed hands just now," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"You think it was that man who came and carried Zhu Ting and the rest away?" said Hua Manlou.
Lu Xiaofeng smiled coldly. "It seems he's still a little uneasy about me, and so has carried off Zhu Ting and the rest, to hold over my head."
"To carry them off in a moment," said Hua Manlou, "his skill can be no less than yours."
Zhu Ting and the Boss's Wife were no mean hands, and with them, besides, was that small imp of great cunning, Shangguan Xue'er.
"I never thought his skill less than mine," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Of men with skill so high," said Hua Manlou, "there aren't many."
"And so he has made a mistake," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"He shouldn't have troubled to do this," said Hua Manlou.
"In doing it," said Lu Xiaofeng, "he has as good as told us who he is."
Hua Manlou sighed. "As I said: every man does wrong sometimes."
"And who does wrong must be punished, one and all alike," said Lu Xiaofeng.

The room was still as a tomb; ten men sat there in silence, watching Lu Xiaofeng. Master Fan the Elder, Master Jian the Second, the Seven Heroes of the Marketplace, and the Shanxi Wild Goose: they had drunk deep, but they drank no more now.
When friends drink together and are not yet drunk, it is hard, as a rule, to stop. But these men were all clear-headed, no flush of wine on any face, and on every face a very strange look.
The Shanxi Wild Goose looked the gravest of all; gazing at Lu Xiaofeng, he said of a sudden, "Can you be truly certain that the man behind it all is he?"
Lu Xiaofeng nodded.
"You're sure of it?" said the Shanxi Wild Goose.
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "We're friends, and I know what he is to you all. Had I not some certainty, why should I've come to you?"

The Shanxi Wild Goose clenched both fists, then brought one down hard of a sudden on the table, and said fiercely, "If Huo Tianqing has truly done this thing, then whatever there is between us, from this day it is at an end!"
Master Fan the Elder said coldly, "But I still don't believe he would do such a thing."
"I couldn't bring myself to believe it either, at first," said Lu Xiaofeng; "but save for him, no second man is to be found."
"Oh?" said Master Fan the Elder.
"He alone could master the three of them, Zhu Ting and the others, in a single moment," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"That reason isn't enough," said Master Fan the Elder.
"He alone could have known the secret of the Golden Roc," said Lu Xiaofeng, "for he was Yan Tieshan's most trusted man."
"That too isn't enough," said Master Fan the Elder.
"He alone stood to gain by it," said Lu Xiaofeng. "Yan Tieshan once dead, the Pavilion of Pearls and Splendour was his."
Yan Tieshan, like Huo Xiu, was an old bachelor; and there was reason enough in the suspicion that he was a eunuch.
"With his standing and his skill," said Lu Xiaofeng, "would he ever have stooped to be steward to a man like Yan Tieshan, had he no further design?"
This even Master Fan the Elder could no longer deny.
"No one in the jianghu would ever dream, of course," said Lu Xiaofeng, "that the First Blue-Robe Tower should lie within the Pavilion of Pearls and Splendour."
The Shanxi Wild Goose's face moved. "You say the First Blue-Robe Tower is within the Pavilion of Pearls and Splendour?"

Lu Xiaofeng nodded. "Dugu Yihe came, plainly, because word of this had reached him; and so Huo Tianqing, on some pretext, first drained away his inner force, and let him die under Ximen Chuixue's sword."
Hua Manlou, who had sat by all the while, could not help saying now, "And Sun Xiuqing and Shi Xiuxue were killed by Shangguan Feiyan to stop their mouths, for that they would have spoken the secret."
"If they knew the secret," said the Shanxi Wild Goose, "how should Ma Xiuzhen and Ye Xiuzhu not have known it?"
"They knew it too," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"But they're still alive," said the Shanxi Wild Goose.
"Ye Xiuzhu is still alive," said Lu Xiaofeng, "only because she too, like Shangguan Feiyan, has lost her heart to the young, handsome, matchless Huo Tianqing."
"And Ma Xiuzhen?" said the Shanxi Wild Goose.
"If I guess aright," said Lu Xiaofeng, "she too has died at Huo Tianqing's hand, and it may even be that Ye Xiuzhu killed her."
"It was to turn you from the scent," said the Shanxi Wild Goose, "that he spoke of the little tower on the mountain behind, and set you to seek Huo Xiu?"
Lu Xiaofeng nodded. "Whether I died in that little tower, or Huo Xiu died by my hand, the matter would be ended either way, and thereafter he might rest easy on a high pillow."
"But he never thought," said the Shanxi Wild Goose, "that you and that solitary old man would prove old friends."
"It was to learn how the matter turned out," said Lu Xiaofeng, "that he set Ye Xiuzhu to wait outside for news."
"And only one person knew you were going to seek Huo Xiu," said the Shanxi Wild Goose.
Lu Xiaofeng nodded again. "But Ye Xiuzhu let one word slip amiss."
"What did she say amiss?" said the Shanxi Wild Goose.
"She said she was staying there only because she had just buried the bodies of Dugu Yihe and Shi Xiuxue," said Lu Xiaofeng.
The Shanxi Wild Goose frowned. "Dugu Yihe was master of a whole sect; how should he be buried so carelessly?"
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "Ye Xiuzhu is, when all's said, a good and virtuous girl; she hasn't yet learned how a lie should be told."
The Shanxi Wild Goose sighed too, and smiled wryly. "To tell a lie before a man like you is no easy thing indeed."

"But I let slip the secret of the six toes before her," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and so she went at once to tell Huo Tianqing; and the Pavilion of Pearls and Splendour and Huo Xiu's little tower stand close by each other."
"So only Huo Tianqing could have had her news so quickly," said the Shanxi Wild Goose.
"Just so," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Did you let the secret slip to her on purpose?" said the Shanxi Wild Goose. "Or unmeaning?"
Lu Xiaofeng did not answer straight, but smiled. "I only felt, at the time, that she had no business appearing there; I only felt it a little strange."
The Shanxi Wild Goose looked at him, sighed again, and smiled wryly. "You should never have been named Lu Xiaofeng, the little phoenix; you're nothing but a little fox."

Lu Xiaofeng sighed too, and smiled wryly. "Yet I admire Huo Tianqing greatly; he is a man of close thought and a cool head. Were this affair a game of chess, his opponent's every move was already within his reckoning."
"The pity is that at the last he made one false move himself," said the Shanxi Wild Goose.
"Every man must err sometimes," said Lu Xiaofeng. "He too is only a man."
Master Fan the Elder smiled coldly of a sudden. "In truth, even had he not made that last move, you would have found him out all the same."
"At least I couldn't have been certain then," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"And now?" said Master Fan the Elder.
"Even now I'm not wholly certain," said Lu Xiaofeng; "nine parts, no more."
"Why have you come to us?" said Master Fan the Elder.
"You're my friends," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and I promised you I would never cross hands with him."
"And now we're friends no longer?" said Master Fan the Elder.
"We're friends still," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and that is why I've come."
"Come to take back your word?" said Master Fan the Elder.
"Whoever does wrong must pay the price, and Huo Tianqing no less," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"You'd have us help you kill him, then?" said Master Fan the Elder.
Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly. "I'd only have you carry him word: tomorrow at sunrise, I wait for him at the Green Wind Temple."
"Very well," said Master Fan the Elder. Of a sudden he sprang into the air, his eyes glaring like a blade's edge at Lu Xiaofeng. "If you please!"
"If you please?" said Lu Xiaofeng. "Please what?"
"Please make your move!" said Master Fan the Elder.
"You don't believe what I've said?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I know only that Huo Tianqing is master of the Heaven's Bird sect," said Master Fan the Elder, "and that I, Fan E, happen to be a disciple of the Heaven's Bird sect."
"And so you—" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"And so, while I, Fan E, live," said Master Fan the Elder, "I can't suffer another to move against Huo Tianqing."
The Shanxi Wild Goose frowned. "'Righteousness before kin'—have you never heard the words?"
Master Fan the Elder said coldly, "I've heard them, and I've forgotten them."
Master Jian the Second rose slowly to his feet as well. "We're men who never told black from white, nor weighed light against heavy."
The bun-seller cried aloud of a sudden, "Such men deserve to die!"
"Just so," said Master Jian the Second. "Richly deserve it."
"The pity is," said the bun-seller, "that I, Bao the Crow, happen to be just such a man."
"And so you deserve to die too," said Master Jian the Second.
"Deserve it I do," said Bao the Crow, "and now's the time for it." Of a sudden he sprang up like a hurled javelin and drove headlong at the wall.
But he did not strike the wall; he struck Lu Xiaofeng's chest, for Lu Xiaofeng had of a sudden come between him and it.

Bao the Crow turned over in the air, kicked off the roof-beam with both legs, and plunged head-down toward the flagstones; but before he struck them he felt a hand press lightly at his waist, and there he was, set squarely on his feet again, face to face with a man, a tall man, straight as jade, and pale of face.
Huo Tianqing.

Every man was struck dumb, Lu Xiaofeng among them; no one had thought Huo Tianqing would appear at this hour of all hours, no one had thought he would dare to come at all. Pale though his face was, Huo Tianqing's bearing was calm still.
Bao the Crow clenched both fists, and said in a shaking voice, "You, why would you not let me die?"
"You deserve to die?" said Huo Tianqing.
"I deserve to die," said Bao the Crow.
Huo Tianqing said coldly, "If you all deserve to die, would you've the whole Heaven's Bird sect wiped out to the last man?"
Bao the Crow was struck dumb at that.
"The Heaven's Bird sect taught you your skill," said Huo Tianqing, "not that you might go seeking your own deaths with it."
"But you—" said Bao the Crow.
Huo Tianqing smiled coldly. "And what am I to you? Were it any other matter, you might all die to the last, and I'd not spare you a glance."
"But now you—" said Bao the Crow.
"Now I only won't have you die for me," said Huo Tianqing. "Were it noised abroad hereafter that a bun-seller had died for my sake, wouldn't I, Huo Tianqing, be the guilty man?"

Of a sudden he drew a bamboo token from his breast, and snapped it in two, and said coldly, "I, Huo Tianqing, have wealth and power, and I've long had no wish to be a poor sect-master. From this day I'm nothing to you or your Heaven's Bird sect; and whoever dares again to call me one of it, I'll cut out his tongue first, and break both his legs after."
Bao the Crow looked at him; of a sudden his eyes went red, and of a sudden he threw himself down on the ground and wept aloud in bitter grief.

The Shanxi Wild Goose's eyes seemed to redden too; but of a sudden he threw back his head and laughed wildly. "Well done, Huo Tianqing. You're worthy of the name of Huo after all; you haven't shamed the word."
Huo Tianqing did not spare them so much as a glance; slowly he turned, and gazed at Lu Xiaofeng, and Lu Xiaofeng gazed back at him.
The two men stood face to face, gazing each at the other; how long passed there was no knowing. Then Lu Xiaofeng sighed of a sudden, long and deep. "Why you? Why, of all men, must it be you?"
Huo Tianqing said coldly, "What I've done, a man like you'll never understand."
"I know you've set your whole heart on some great, earth-shaking deed," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and wouldn't live out your life in your father's shadow; but a thing like this—"
Huo Tianqing said fiercely, "This is that great deed. Save I, Huo Tianqing, who could have done it?"
Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly. "No other, truly."

"And save you," said Huo Tianqing, "no other could have wrecked my great deed." Of a sudden he threw back his head with a long sigh. "In a world that holds Huo Tianqing, there should be no Lu Xiaofeng."
"And so—" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"And so between us two," said Huo Tianqing, "one must die; only which shall it be, you or I?"
Lu Xiaofeng sighed, long and deep. "Tomorrow at sunrise, perhaps, we'll know."

Huo Tianqing smiled coldly. "There is a tomorrow after every tomorrow; why not change our tryst from tomorrow to today?" Of a sudden he flicked his sleeve, and was already beyond the door; only his cold voice came from far off: "This very dusk, I wait for you outside the Green Wind Temple."
Dusk. The Green Wind Temple. The Green Wind Temple stood on the green mountain, and the green mountain lay now beyond the slanting sun.

There was no mist, only a thin drift of white cloud, floating, that looked for all the world like mist. A gust of wind passed, and the dusk-crows started up among the grey pines; the last streak of slanting sun in the western sky grew fainter. Then the twilight lay over all the earth. Facing the boundless dusk that filled the mountains, Lu Xiaofeng's heart was heavier even than the dusk.
Hua Manlou too seemed sunk in a bleak humour, and said with a sigh, "Huo Tianqing hasn't come yet."
"He is sure to come," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I'd never have thought him such a man," said Hua Manlou. "He should never have done such a thing."
Lu Xiaofeng said, low and sorrowful, "And yet do it he did."
"That may be only because he is too proud," said Hua Manlou; "he wouldn't only best all other men, but best his own father as well."
"Pride is a foolish thing at bottom," said Lu Xiaofeng.
A man too proud will do foolish things, and there is no help for it.
"And it is his pride, too," said Hua Manlou, "that he'll not shirk the burden of what he's done."
Lu Xiaofeng was long silent, then asked of a sudden, "Were you in my place, would you let him go?"
"I'm not you," said Hua Manlou.
Lu Xiaofeng heaved a long sigh. "As well you aren't me; and as well, too, that I'm not you."

Hua Manlou said no more, for by now he had heard the sound of a door opening. The old, heavy gate of the Green Wind Temple had just swung a crack apart. A yellow-robed Taoist boy came out, a lantern in his hand, and behind him came another; but it was not Huo Tianqing, it was a Taoist priest in a yellow robe.

The priest wore wide robes and great sleeves; the hair at both temples was streaked with grey, and his look was very grave. His step was light and easy, yet he seemed no man who had trained in the martial arts. He glanced about him, then came straight to Lu Xiaofeng, and made his bow. "Is the patron perhaps the young lord Lu Xiaofeng?"
Lu Xiaofeng nodded. "And you, Reverend, are—"
"This poor priest is Qingfeng," said the Taoist, "abbot of this little temple."
"Are you a friend of Huo Tianqing's, Reverend?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"The patron Huo and I are friends over the chessboard," said Qingfeng; "every month he comes to stay with me a few days."
"And where is he now?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
A very strange look came over Qingfeng's face again. "I've come," he said, "for that very purpose: to bring the patron to see him."
"Where is he?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"He waits in my cloud-chamber," said Qingfeng slowly, "and has waited this good while."
The little court was strangely still; from a half-open window, incense-smoke drifted, thin, and scattered on the wind; the door too stood ajar.
Lu Xiaofeng crossed the little court; and when Qingfeng pushed the door open, he saw Huo Tianqing—but Huo Tianqing would never see him again.

Huo Tianqing lay dead on the cloud-couch in the Taoist Qingfeng's chamber; and on a low table by the couch stood a cup carved from green jade in the shape of a coiling dragon, with a little wine left in it, poisoned wine.
Huo Tianqing's face was ashen; at the corners of his eyes, his mouth, his nose, one could still faintly make out where blood had been wiped clean away. Lu Xiaofeng looked at him, and his heart sank.

The Taoist Qingfeng's face was very bleak, and he said, low and sorrowful, "When he came, I took it he had come to finish yesterday's unfinished game; I was waiting to see what fine new move he might have to slip past that peril on the board. But he said he had no heart for chess today."
"He wanted only to drink?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Qingfeng nodded. "It was then I saw that something was amiss in his look, as though some weight lay on his mind; and he sighed without cease, long and short, and muttered to himself."
"What did he say?" said Lu Xiaofeng.

"He seemed to be saying that a man's span of a hundred years passes in the blink of an eye," said Qingfeng, "and saying, too, that since the world had a Huo Tianqing in it, why must there be a Lu Xiaofeng besides."
Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly, yet could not help asking, "Was it you who made the wine ready for him?"
"The wine was of this house," said Qingfeng, "but the cup he brought himself; he had a horror of uncleanness, and would never use a thing another had used."
Lu Xiaofeng took up the cup and smelled it, and frowned. "So the poison was on the cup after all."

"Several times he took the cup up and set it down again," said Qingfeng, "as though he had met a hard problem on the board and couldn't decide his move. I was wondering at it when of a sudden he threw back his head, laughed aloud three times, and drank the cup dry." The care-laden priest pressed his palms together, and said, low and sorrowful, "I never thought that one so young had already seen through the ways of the world. May he find the Way's mountain soon." His voice sank lower and lower as he spoke, and it seemed there were tears about to fall from his eyes.
Lu Xiaofeng was silent, his heart heavier still; and after a long while he sighed. "He named no one else?"
"No one," said Qingfeng.
"Nor spoke the name of Zhu Ting?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"No," said Qingfeng.

Beside the cloud-couch a half-finished game of chess was set out. The Taoist Qingfeng murmured, "The affairs of the world are without constancy, changing as white clouds into grey dogs; who could have thought this unfinished game would still be here, and the man who played it gone?"
Lu Xiaofeng said of a sudden, "He played the black stones?"
"I always gave him a stone's handicap," said Qingfeng.
Lu Xiaofeng picked up a black stone, pondered, and set it down slowly. "I'll play this game for him."
Qingfeng smiled sorrowfully. "With that stone laid down, black has lost."
"But he had no other road left," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"This game he had already lost," said Qingfeng, "and he knew it himself; only he would never own himself beaten."
Lu Xiaofeng gazed into the distance, and murmured, "But now, when all's said, he has owned himself beaten. The board is a life; one move gone wrong, and the game is surely lost."

Of a sudden Qingfeng swept his sleeve across the unfinished game and scattered it, and said, drawn out and slow, "And isn't a life just such a game of chess? Why take the winning and the losing so much to heart?"
"If a man takes it not to heart," said Lu Xiaofeng, "why sit down to play the game at all?"
Qingfeng gave him a glance, pressed his palms together, and slowly closed his eyes, and said no more. A gust of wind blew the window open; the night lay over all the earth now.
Lu Xiaofeng lay on the bed, gazing at a cup of wine on his chest. The cup had rested there a long while, and to this moment he had not drunk it; he seemed to have no heart even for wine.
"Are you thinking of Zhu Ting and the rest?" said Hua Manlou.
Lu Xiaofeng was silent.

"When a man is near death, his heart turns kind," said Hua Manlou. "Since Huo Tianqing had set his mind on dying, surely he would work no more evil, kill no more; and by now they may well be safe home again."
The words were meant to comfort Lu Xiaofeng, and to comfort himself as well. But Lu Xiaofeng seemed not to have heard.
Hua Manlou forced a smile. "However it be, this game at least you've won."
Lu Xiaofeng heaved a long sigh of a sudden. "But this last move wasn't mine to make."
"Not even played to your own design?" said Hua Manlou.
"No," said Lu Xiaofeng.
He smiled wryly, and went on: "And so, though I've won this game, it sits worse with me than losing would."
Hua Manlou too could not help a long sigh. "Why would he not play this last game out to the end?"
"Because he knew himself the game already lost," said Lu Xiaofeng, "just as he wouldn't play out that other game yesterday—"
The words were scarcely out when of a sudden he sprang up from the bed, and the wine-cup on his chest fell with a "clang" to the floor and shattered to bits.

Hua Manlou knew that he never let a wine-cup of his own be broken. But now he seemed to have forgotten that wholly; he stood there like a man out of his wits, feeling his whole body gone cold, cold from his head down to the soles of his feet.
Hua Manlou did not ask him why; Hua Manlou knew he would say it of himself.
Lu Xiaofeng said of a sudden, "Yesterday too he didn't finish that game?"
"Just so," said Hua Manlou.
"Yesterday he was here at the Green Wind Temple, playing chess," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Hua Manlou's face changed too.
"If Shangguan Feiyan died at his hand," said Lu Xiaofeng, "how could he have been here playing chess yesterday?"
Shangguan Feiyan was hundreds of li away; had Huo Tianqing wings, he could not have flown back within a single day. And it was yesterday that Shangguan Feiyan died.
Hua Manlou felt his own hands and feet go cold, and said with a sigh, "Can we've wronged him, then?"
Lu Xiaofeng clenched both fists. "At the least, it was never he who killed Shangguan Feiyan." Hua Manlou nodded.
"In this one thing, at least, we wronged him," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Why did he not defend himself?" said Hua Manlou.

"He set our meeting here at the Green Wind Temple," said Lu Xiaofeng, "perhaps for this very reason: that the priest might bear witness he had been here at the Green Wind Temple playing chess yesterday."
"Because he knew that a defence in bare words you'd never have believed," said Hua Manlou.
"The pity is he never had the chance to make it," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Then he didn't die by his own will, of course?" said Hua Manlou.
"Never," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Who killed him, then?" said Hua Manlou.
"The man who killed him," said Lu Xiaofeng, "is the same who killed Shangguan Feiyan."
"And he is the true master-hand behind it all?" said Hua Manlou.
"Just so," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"The Taoist Qingfeng has been bought by him too," said Hua Manlou, "and so lies for him."
"A man of religion is a man still," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"In that case, the Taoist Qingfeng must surely know who he is!" said Hua Manlou.
Lu Xiaofeng sighed, long and deep. "And so now I hope only that Qingfeng is still alive."
He was disappointed. When they came back to the Green Wind Temple, the Green Wind Temple had turned to a sea of fire; no one had got out of it, not a single soul.
Fire is without mercy, and the man who set this fire more merciless still. Who was he?
The Green Wind Temple stood on the front of the mountain, and Huo Xiu's little tower behind it; and though the front of the mountain had become a sea of fire, the back of it was peaceful and still.

The word Push was on the door still; Lu Xiaofeng pushed it open, and he and Hua Manlou, the two of them, went in. It was the second time he had pushed this door open, and perhaps the last. The belly of the mountain was empty, nothing left in it; those pearls and treasures and arms beyond all counting had, as by a miracle, wholly vanished. In the midst of the mountain's belly was a small stone platform spread with an old straw mat, and there, barefoot, in a suit of blue cloth washed white with age, Huo Xiu sat cross-legged, warming wine. Fine-scented wine.
Lu Xiaofeng drew a long breath, went down the stone steps, and said with a smile, "It seems I've come at just the right time this time too."
Huo Xiu smiled too. "But this time I'm no longer surprised; let me but have good wine, and you'll come seeking me."
"And yet I've come to have my doubts," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Doubts of what?" said Huo Xiu.
"Doubts as to whether you lured me here with good wine on purpose," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu laughed aloud. "Be that as it may, good wine is good wine; if you don't mind dirtying your clothes, you may still sit down and have a cup."
"I do mind," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu frowned. "You mind?"
"It's not the dirtying of my clothes I mind," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"What is it, then?" said Huo Xiu.
"I mind lest, like Huo Tianqing, once I drink this cup I must wait for another to clear away the unfinished game," said Lu Xiaofeng.

Huo Xiu looked at him, and his gaze became like a blade drawn from its sheath. He said no more, only poured a cup of wine slowly and drank it slowly down. Lu Xiaofeng too said no more; he knew the words were enough. It was a clever man he faced, and to a clever man a single word is enough. How long passed there was no knowing; then of a sudden Huo Xiu laughed aloud. "It seems there's no hiding it from you after all."
"So you need hide it no longer," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"How did you come to think it was me?" said Huo Xiu.
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "I never thought of it; from the very first I was wrong."
"Oh?" said Huo Xiu.
"I always took you for one of the wronged, like Yan Tieshan and Dugu Yihe," said Lu Xiaofeng; "I always thought that only Huo Tianqing could gain by the affair."
"And now?" said Huo Xiu.
"Now I've thought it through," said Lu Xiaofeng: "the one man who could truly gain by it is one alone."
"And that man is I," said Huo Xiu.
"Just so," said Lu Xiaofeng. "That man is you."
Huo Xiu poured another cup of wine.
"The Great King of the Golden Roc once dead," said Lu Xiaofeng, "there'd be no one left in the world to press you for the old debt of the Golden Roc."
Huo Xiu nodded slowly. "He'd never have pressed me for it, as a rule; but of late years he had grown too poor. He was a man who knew well how to spend, and never how hard it is to earn."
"And so you had to kill him?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu said coldly, "Such men deserve to die."
"But his death wasn't enough," said Lu Xiaofeng, "for Dugu Yihe and Yan Tieshan would still have come to share the fortune."
"The fortune was mine from the first," said Huo Xiu. "I alone toiled and moiled to guard it, and made it grow greater day by day; I'll let no man share it."
"And so they too deserved to die?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Die they must," said Huo Xiu.
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "Yet thirty men couldn't spend that fortune to its end. You're so old now; do you mean to carry it into the coffin with you?"
Huo Xiu glared at him, and said coldly, "If you had a wife, you'd have no use for her by day in any case; but would you let another share her with you?"
"These are two wholly different things," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu said, "To my mind the two things are exactly one. This fortune is like a wife to me; alive or dead, I'll never let another make use of it."
"And so you first used Huo Tianqing and Shangguan Feiyan to kill the Great King of the Golden Roc," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and then used me to rid you of Dugu Yihe and Yan Tieshan."
"I'd not have sought you out," said Huo Xiu, "but that, save for you, I could think of no second man to do the thing."
Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly. "I've heard that said before."
"It's the plain truth," said Huo Xiu.
"It was of my own free will I took your hook," said Lu Xiaofeng; "but Huo Tianqing? How should a man like him be used by you?"
"It wasn't I who hooked him," said Huo Xiu.
"Shangguan Feiyan, then?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu smiled. "Do you not find her a woman well able to stir a man's heart?" Hua Manlou smiled wryly.
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "And how did you move her heart?"
Huo Xiu said easily, "Old man though I'm, I can stir a woman's heart as well as any; for I've a thing no woman can refuse."
"And what thing is that?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"My jewels," said Huo Xiu. He smiled, and added lightly, "There is no woman in the world who loves not jewels, just as there is no man who loves not a beautiful woman."
"You promised Shangguan Feiyan a share of your jewels," said Lu Xiaofeng, "to have her lure Huo Tianqing?"
Huo Xiu laughed aloud. "You all took her lover for Huo Tianqing, and never thought that the one she loved was this old man here."
Lu Xiaofeng could not help reminding him, "It wasn't you she loved either, but your jewels."
Huo Xiu laughed. "It comes to the same thing; in my eyes she was a dead woman long since, in any case."
"You had meant, the thing once done, to kill her and stop her mouth?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I've said it: my fortune I'll let no man share," said Huo Xiu.
"And so you told me the secret of the six toes on purpose," said Lu Xiaofeng, "to set me to kill her?"
"But Huo Tianqing was still in the dark," said Huo Xiu, "and so, in his haste, he sent word of the secret to Shangguan Feiyan by carrier-pigeon."
"Even he didn't know that you were the true master-hand behind it all?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Of course he didn't," said Huo Xiu; "else how should he have given himself heart and soul to serve Shangguan Feiyan?"
"But you never thought that I would let Shangguan Feiyan go," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"And so I had to see to it myself," said Huo Xiu.

"Huo Tianqing was no fool either," said Lu Xiaofeng. "Hearing of Shangguan Feiyan's death, he too saw that there must be a master-hand behind it all; and so, after fixing our meeting at the Green Wind Temple, he first hastened here to you."
"He wasn't overly foolish, it's true," said Huo Xiu; "but the pity is that clever men will often do foolish things."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "He should never have come to you alone."
"And so he too deserved to die," said Huo Xiu.
"And having killed him, you had him borne to the Green Wind Temple?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"The land the Green Wind Temple stands on is mine too," said Huo Xiu; "I can take it back whenever I please."
"And so when you had the Taoist Qingfeng lie for you, he dared not refuse," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu said easily, "A man of religion, and he lies; of course he deserved to die too."
"You had meant me to think Huo Tianqing had died in fear of his guilt," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and meant me to stay my hand at that."
Huo Xiu sighed. "I truly wanted you to meddle in it no further; the pity is that the chattering priest was your undoing."
"My undoing?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"When I heard him speak of yesterday's unfinished game," said Huo Xiu, "I knew you'd hit sooner or later on that flaw."
"And so you set the Green Wind Temple ablaze, and had done," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I happened to have another use for the land besides," said Huo Xiu.
"To your eyes, then, all these people are just like that patch of land," said Lu Xiaofeng, "no more than tools for your using?"
"So that if I would have them live, they live," said Huo Xiu; "and if I would have them die, die they must."
Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly. "How did you think to use even me?"
"Every man has his weak point," said Huo Xiu; "know a man's weak point, and any man alike may be used."
"And what is my weak point?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu said coldly, "Your weak point is that you love too well to meddle in what is no affair of yours."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "And so I became your accomplice, went to make the tryst with Ximen Chuixue for you, and helped you rid yourself of Yan Tieshan and Dugu Yihe."

"You did it all very well," said Huo Xiu. "Once Huo Tianqing was dead, had you been willing to stay your hand, you might still have come to drink my good wine whenever you pleased; and were you ever in straits, I might even, it may be, have lent you ten thousand taels or so."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "The pity is I haven't stayed my hand yet."
Huo Xiu sighed too. "Do you know why I had everything here carried away?"
Lu Xiaofeng did not know.
"Because I mean to keep this place," said Huo Xiu, "for your grave."
Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly. "A grave of no small size, truly."
Huo Xiu said easily, "To lie buried beneath the First Blue-Robe Tower, Lu Xiaofeng may well die without a regret."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "Shangguan Feiyan told one truth at least: the First Blue-Robe Tower is here indeed."
"The pity is that the more others said the First Blue-Robe Tower was here," said Huo Xiu, "the less you would believe it."
"You're the Grand Helmsman, then, of the one hundred and eight Blue-Robe Towers?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu smiled. "'Grand Helmsman'—there is a fine ring to those four words; I like the sound of them."
"Finer even than the sound of your counting money?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I don't count my money," said Huo Xiu lightly; "my money is past all counting."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed again. "Now at last I truly understand how you came to be rich."
"Understand it you may," said Huo Xiu, "but the pity is you'll never learn it in all your life."
"I've no wish to carry my money into the coffin," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu laughed aloud. "Good. Very good."
"Very good?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu laughed. "They say you always carry a thick sheaf of banknotes on you, and that when you spend, it's five thousand taels at the least."
Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly. "Those five thousand taels of banknotes are in your own purse by now, I fear."
"Since you'd not carry your money into the coffin," said Huo Xiu, "once you're dead I'll be sure to take the banknotes out for you."
"You'd take even a dead man's money?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Money of any kind I'll take," said Huo Xiu; "that too is one of the secrets of growing rich."
"The pity is I'm still alive," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"But you're in your grave already," said Huo Xiu.
"You're sure you can kill me?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Whoever goes into the grave," said Huo Xiu, "let him not dream of coming out alive again."
Lu Xiaofeng looked at him, and a light like a blade's edge came into his eyes too.
Huo Xiu smiled. "Are your hands itching for it already?"
"They do itch a little, it's true," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu said easily, "The pity is I've no mind to cross hands with you; I never did like to trade blows with a man as good as dead."
He pressed a hand lightly on the stone platform; and of a sudden, with a crash, a huge iron cage came down from above and closed over the platform.
Lu Xiaofeng frowned. "When did you turn into a bird? Why cage yourself up?"
"You find it droll?" said Huo Xiu.
"Droll indeed," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Once I've gone you'll not find it droll," said Huo Xiu; "when a man knows he's soon to starve to death, he'll find nothing droll at all."
"I'm soon to starve to death?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu said coldly, "Once I'm gone, the only thing here fit to eat will be the flesh of you and your friend, and the only thing to drink your own blood."
"But how will you get out?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"The one way out of this place," said Huo Xiu, "lies beneath the very platform I sit on; and I can promise you that, once I've gone, I'll not forget to seal it up behind me."
Lu Xiaofeng's face changed a little; he forced a smile. "It wasn't by that way I came in, it seems."
"The door you came in by opens only from without," said Huo Xiu, "and I can promise you too that no one will open it for you from the outside."
"And what else can you promise?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I can promise you'll die of thirst inside ten days," said Huo Xiu; "only, I've always been a careful man, so I'll be sure to wait ten days more before I come back."
"You'll come back?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu smiled. "Of course I'll come back—to take the banknotes off you."
Lu Xiaofeng laughed. "Do you know that all there's left in my pocket now is a great hole?"
Huo Xiu sighed. "It seems you're set on giving me not the least advantage, even in dying."
"You've come to see it at last," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"As luck would have it, there's an advantage to be had yet," said Huo Xiu.
"Oh?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I can at least strip the clothes off your backs," said Huo Xiu, "and sell them to a second-hand stall; that'll fetch a few cash, at the least."
"You'd take even a few cash?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Money is always good," said Huo Xiu; "a few cash is better than none."
"Very well, I'll give you some," said Lu Xiaofeng. His hand swept out of a sudden, and a dozen-odd bronze coins, driven on a rush of wind, flew at Huo Xiu.

Huo Xiu neither stirred nor gave way; he waited only until the coins had passed through the bars of the iron cage, then gave a beckon of his hand, and all twelve coins dropped of a sudden into his palm. So marvellous was the old man's hand-work that even Lu Xiaofeng, seeing it, could not but be moved, and the words broke from him: "Fine work!"
Huo Xiu had gathered up the twelve coins with the greatest care, and said with a smile, "When there's money to be gathered, my hand-work is always especially good."
"The pity is that this hand-work of yours falls a little short of mine," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu laughed aloud. "Are you trying to goad me out to fight you?"
"That was my thought, I confess," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Then I'd counsel you to put the notion by, and quickly," said Huo Xiu.
"You'll not come out, then, though you die for it?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Even had I a mind to come out," said Huo Xiu, "I couldn't, now."
"Why not?" said Lu Xiaofeng.

"This iron cage is cast of tempered steel," said Huo Xiu, "and weighs 1,980 catties net. Not even a blade that cuts iron like mud could be sure of cutting through it, and blades of that kind are to be found only in the tales of myth."
"An iron cage of 1,980 catties," said Lu Xiaofeng, "no man could lift, to be sure."
"None could," said Huo Xiu.
"So that not only can you not come out," said Lu Xiaofeng, "but I can't get in."
"So all you can do is watch me go, and then wait to starve," said Huo Xiu.
"You shut yourself up in this cage first," said Lu Xiaofeng, "for fear I'd come at you to fight?"
"I'm an old man," said Huo Xiu; "I've lost even the taste for a woman's bed, let alone for fighting."
Lu Xiaofeng patted Hua Manlou on the shoulder, and sighed. "It seems there's nothing left for us but to wait for death."
Hua Manlou, for a wonder, smiled. "It seems this is his last move," he said lightly.
"You can't deny," said Lu Xiaofeng, "that it's a very deadly move indeed."
"But we've a move yet unplayed," said Hua Manlou; "there is one man still in our hand."
"Oh?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Have you forgotten Zhu Ting?" said Hua Manlou.
Lu Xiaofeng smiled. "I haven't forgotten."
Hua Manlou smiled. "And that is why you can still smile, even now."
"And why you aren't the least bit anxious," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"He should never have carried Zhu Ting here as well," said Hua Manlou.
"He shouldn't, indeed," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu's face seemed to have changed a little; he could not help saying, "And what if Zhu Ting is here?"
"Nothing at all," said Lu Xiaofeng lightly; "only that there isn't yet, in all the world, a place that can hold him."
"The man has no other gift," said Hua Manlou, "save that he happens to be Master Lu's disciple."
Huo Xiu frowned. "Master Lu?"
"You must surely know," said Hua Manlou, "that Master Lu is a descendant of the patriarch Lu Ban, and the first hand under all heaven at the making of hidden contrivances."
"And since Master Lu died," said Lu Xiaofeng, "that first hand is Zhu Ting, the Boss."
"So that as long as he is here," said Huo Xiu, "you're certain to get out?"
"Just so," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"He is here indeed," said Huo Xiu.
"I know," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"In the place behind, where you saw me last," said Huo Xiu.
"I know," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"If there's no place in the world that can hold him," said Huo Xiu, "then why has he not come out yet?"
"He'll come out," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu smiled. "Even could he come out now, it's too late already."
"Oh?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"The master-spring of all the contrivances in this place," said Huo Xiu, "is beneath the very spot I sit on."
"Oh?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"The moment I go out, I'll destroy it, of course, on the instant," said Huo Xiu.
"And then?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"And then every way out of this place will be sealed at once with stone blocks," said Huo Xiu, "each block of them above eight thousand catties in weight; and so—"
"And so we must die here, past all help?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Xiu said lightly, "You two aside, were Lu Ban himself born again, he could only wait here to die a second time."
"And so you'll be going now?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I'd have liked to sit and talk with you here a while longer," said Huo Xiu; "I know that waiting for death is no pleasant thing."
"But now you've changed your mind?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Just so," said Huo Xiu.
"It seems I can neither keep you here nor see you off," said Lu Xiaofeng.

"But you'll soon be missing me, I'm sure of it," said Huo Xiu. He reached out a hand, smiling, and went on, "The moment I press my hand down, I'll be gone; and never after this will you set eyes on me again."
He pressed his hand down; but he did not vanish. It was the smile on his face that vanished.

The four-square stone platform was a four-square stone platform still. He had been sitting bolt upright upon it, and he sat bolt upright upon it yet; and the look on his face was as though someone had of a sudden dealt him a blow on the nose.

Beads of sweat, each bigger than a soybean, sprang out of a sudden on his brow. Lu Xiaofeng found it strange too; he knew Huo Xiu well, and the old fox never did a thing he was not wholly sure of. If Huo Xiu said there was a way out beneath the stone platform, then beneath the stone platform there was surely a way out; but now, that way out seemed of a sudden to have vanished.
Lu Xiaofeng blinked. "Why have you not gone yet?"
Huo Xiu clenched both fists. "You—you—" He did not finish the words; he had fainted away.

Lu Xiaofeng sighed; and of a sudden he found that someone else was sighing besides himself. The sighers were not Hua Manlou, but Shangguan Xue'er and the Boss's Wife, who came forward sighing, with smiles like spring flowers on their faces.
Shangguan Xue'er said, "It seems you were right; the man has a trick or two in him after all."
The Boss's Wife smiled the sweeter. "And that is why there is but one Lu Xiaofeng, and no second!"
But Lu Xiaofeng could not help a wry smile. "You held back all this while just to see whether I'd a trick or two left in me?"
Shangguan Xue'er smiled sweetly. "We'd thought you'd surely no way left this time to deal with the old fox; and who'd have known you had a last move in reserve?"
The Boss's Wife tittered. "That last move of yours was a marvel indeed."
Shangguan Xue'er said, "This cage he'd meant for you; never in his dreams, I'll warrant, did he think he'd be the one shut up in it."
Lu Xiaofeng laughed too. "This move is what they call 'inviting the ruler into the urn.'"
The Boss's Wife looked at him, her eyes like flowing water. "However did you hit on so cunning a stroke?"
Lu Xiaofeng said easily, "Why, I'm a genius born."
Shangguan Xue'er said, "Do you mean that, before ever you came in, you reckoned he'd go out by that way, and sealed the way up first?"
Lu Xiaofeng said nothing.
The Boss's Wife too could not help asking, "Why won't you speak? What way did you use, when all's said?"
Lu Xiaofeng shook his head of a sudden. "I can't tell you."
"Why not?" said Shangguan Xue'er.

Lu Xiaofeng smiled. "Every man must keep a trick or two of his own in reserve; and least of all should he give them away before women like you." His smile had grown a little like an old fox's too. Of a sudden he went on, "If you learned all my best tricks, what good days should I've left?"
When there was no one by, Hua Manlou too could not help asking him, "What way did you use, when all's said? Why would you not tell them?"
Lu Xiaofeng's answer was a fine one: "Because I don't know myself."
Hua Manlou was taken aback. "You don't know either, how the way out came to be sealed of a sudden?"
"I don't know," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Hua Manlou was struck dumb.

"Perhaps the mechanism simply failed of a sudden," said Lu Xiaofeng; "perhaps a rat blundered in by chance and jammed the spring." A faint, musing look came into his eyes too; and he sighed. "What was the true cause of it? No one knows. Heaven alone knows, I fear."
"Heaven alone knows?" said Hua Manlou.
Lu Xiaofeng nodded. "Do you know why it is that the doers of evil always fail at the very last?"
"I don't," said Hua Manlou.
"Because Heaven has long since made ready a last move of its own," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and waits there with it for them; and so, however cunning their schemes, it comes to nothing all the same."
"So this last move too," said Hua Manlou, "wasn't yours to make, but the will of Heaven."
"Just so," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Hua Manlou smiled of a sudden.
"What are you smiling at?" said Lu Xiaofeng. "You don't believe it?"
Hua Manlou laughed. "Did you truly think I would?"
Lu Xiaofeng sighed, and smiled wryly. "Why is it that when I tell the truth, no one will ever believe me?"
